qadash (Hiphil) קָדַשׁ qadash — to sanctify, to demonstrate as holy In the Hiphil stem, the causative form: to cause something or someone to be recognized as holy; to communicate or demonstrate the holiness and integrity of God to others. In Numbers 20:12, God's charge against Moses is that he failed to communicate the divine integrity to the congregation — not merely that he failed a ritual sanctification.
Logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the physical existence and continued spiritual functioning of the believer in phase two. Includes food, shelter, health, transportation, occupation, doctrine, and all testing necessary for spiritual growth. Provided by the justice of God imputing to the righteousness of God resident in the believer, without reference to the believer's merit or spiritual condition.
Adjustment to the justice of God The mechanism by which all divine blessing is received. Three categories: salvation adjustment (faith in Christ, once for all); rebound adjustment (naming known sins to God, restoring fellowship, 1 John 1:9); and maturity adjustment (progressive advance through sustained doctrine intake, culminating in supergrace).
GAP — Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received, understood, and internalized. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit and positive volition toward the Word of God. Produces epignosis — the exact, operational knowledge of divine truth that develops capacity for blessing.
Reversionism Retroactive spiritual regression — the condition of a believer who has returned to the thinking, values, and patterns of the old sin nature. The reversionist retains imputed righteousness and continues to receive logistical support from the justice of God; discipline addresses the reversionism itself.
Old sin nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line. Resident in every human being, believer and unbeliever alike. Produces both the area of weakness (personal sins) and the area of strength (self-righteousness). Not eradicated at salvation; controlled through the filling of the Holy Spirit.
Supergrace / Ultra-supergrace The stages of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier. In the supergrace condition, the justice of God imputes special blessing — blessing above and beyond logistical support — to the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer. Ultra-supergrace designates the highest stage of maturity in phase two, productive of maximum glorification of God and eternal reward.

Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Four

Romans 10:3 — Submission to the Righteousness of God

Romans 10:3 “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For not knowing the righteousness of God, and by seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not been obedient to the righteousness of God.

This chapter continues the exegesis of Romans 10, where Paul addresses the spiritual condition of Israel. Verse 3 is the doctrinal center of this section: the contrast between the righteousness that God imputes by grace and the self-righteousness that human arrogance constructs in its place. The verse applies both to the Jewish unbeliever who has rejected Christ and to the born-again believer who possesses divine righteousness yet attempts to compete with it through legalism and moralism.

I. Grammatical and Lexical Analysis of Romans 10:3

The opening clause, 'For not knowing the righteousness of God,' establishes the cognitive deficiency at the root of Israel's failure. The knowledge in view is not mere intellectual awareness but the precise, exact perception expressed by the term epignosis — the category of knowledge required for genuine spiritual orientation. Israel's ignorance is not the ignorance of those who have never heard; it is the willful ignorance of those who have heard and refused to internalize.

A. The Negative Adverb and the Verb Hupotassō

The verse begins with the negative adverb ou (οὐ), used with the indicative mood to make a declarative denial of fact. The main verb is the aorist passive indicative of hupotassō (ὑποτάσσω), a military term meaning to be subordinate, to be placed in rank under an authority. The passive voice denotes the result of an act of will: these individuals were not caused to be subordinate — that is, they actively refused submission. The culminative aorist views the entire history of the Jewish rejection of the gospel as a completed whole, regarding it from the standpoint of its existing result.

The verb hupotassō is a compound of hupo (under) and tassō (to arrange, to assign a place). In the military context from which Paul draws the term, it signifies the discipline of occupying one's assigned position under the command structure. Applied here, it means to occupy one's proper position under the authority of God's imputed righteousness. The correct translation of the final clause is: they have not been obedient to the righteousness of God.

B. The Righteousness of God: Dikaiosynē Theou

With the verb we have the dative singular of reference from the noun dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη), together with the possessive genitive of the noun theos (θεός). The phrase dikaiosynē theou — the righteousness of God — is the central subject of the Epistle to the Romans and the organizing axis of the entire adjustment to the justice of God. It is not an attribute that God admires in us; it is His own perfect righteousness, imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ.

The complete corrected translation of verse 3 reads: For not knowing the righteousness of God, and by seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not been obedient to the righteousness of God.

C. Rejection of Spiritual Authority

Israel's failure to submit to divine righteousness is framed in verse 3 as a failure of authority orientation. The gospel had been communicated to the Jewish people through three distinct categories of spiritual authority:

First, the Apostle Paul — the highest category of delegated spiritual authority in the Church Age, with authority over all local churches. Second, pastor-teachers, whose spiritual gift carries authority within the local assembly to communicate Bible doctrine. Third, evangelists, whose gift carries authority outside the local church to communicate the gospel to unbelievers directly. All three categories had presented the redemptive work of the Lord Jesus Christ and the offer of God's imputed righteousness. Israel's rejection of the gospel was therefore simultaneously a rejection of the entire structure of divinely authorized spiritual communication.

II. The Integrity of God and Logistical Grace

The exegesis of verse 3 opens onto one of the foundational principles of the faith-rest technique: the integrity of God is the issue in logistical grace. At the moment of salvation the justice of God imputes the righteousness of God to the believer. This act establishes a grace pipeline and simultaneously creates a new divine obligation — not an obligation contingent on the believer's performance, but one grounded in the integrity of God Himself.

God cannot deny His own righteousness. Because the believer possesses divine righteousness — not earned, not deserved, not produced by any human effort — the justice of God is committed to providing whatever logistical support is necessary to sustain that believer's life on earth. This commitment is unconditional with respect to the believer's spiritual status. The mature believer receives logistical support. The reversionist receives logistical support. The carnal believer receives logistical support. The sole qualification is the possession of divine righteousness, which every believer received at the moment of faith in Christ.

A. The Second Meribah Incident: Moses and the Integrity of God

The incident recorded in Numbers 20 provides the clearest negative illustration of this principle. Israel was without water. Rather than claiming the promises of God and making the integrity of God the public issue, Moses struck the rock twice, addressing the congregation in anger and calling them rebels. God provided the water regardless — because the issue in logistical grace is the integrity of God, not the behavior of the recipient. Even in the midst of nearly universal failure of the faith-rest technique, God sustained the nation.

The tragedy was not that water failed to appear. Water appeared. The tragedy was that Moses, a mature believer operating under supergrace blessing, obscured the real issue. Instead of announcing that God would sustain them because of His own integrity and because they possessed His righteousness, Moses drew attention to the congregation's failure and to his own role in the provision. The statement 'must we fetch water out of the rock?' placed the emphasis on human instrumentality rather than divine integrity. The consequence was that Moses forfeited the privilege of leading Israel into the land — not because God withdrew logistical grace, but because Moses had violated the very principle he was commissioned to exemplify.

Moses could have said: None of us is worthy of this provision. But God will give us water because we are His people, because we possess His righteousness, and because His integrity demands that He sustain us. That was the content that the moment required. The failure to deliver it cost Moses the land. He died under dying grace, with all the blessings of supergrace intact, and will receive greater eternal rewards than virtually any other figure in Scripture. But the discipline was real and the principle was recorded for every subsequent generation.

B. Logistical Blessing versus Supergrace Blessing

A necessary distinction governs this passage. In logistical grace blessing, the only issue is the integrity of God. All believers — advancing, regressing, carnal, mature — receive logistical support because all possess divine righteousness. The warehouses of divine provision have no shortage; the supply is governed by God's integrity, not the believer's performance. Food, shelter, clothing, transportation, freedom — whatever is necessary to sustain life and to give the believer the opportunity either to advance to maturity or to pass through the progressive stages of reversionism — God provides.

Supergrace blessing operates on a different principle. The six categories of special divine blessing are imputed to the righteousness of God in the mature believer — the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier through sustained intake and application of Bible doctrine. The status quo of the believer is the issue in supergrace. Logistical blessing is unconditional with respect to spiritual status; supergrace blessing is conditional upon spiritual advance.

Grace is the policy of the justice of God in imputing divine blessing to the righteousness of God. Logistical blessing is one expression of that policy — available to all believers. Special blessing is the other expression — available to mature believers. God disciplines even the mature believer, as illustrated by Moses at Meribah, but divine discipline is itself an expression of logistical grace: it is God taking responsibility for the believer's life and its outcomes.

C. Authority Orientation and the Believer's Privacy

The military verb hupotassō introduces the broader theme of authority orientation. No one can be rightly oriented to the realities of life who has not come to terms with the authorities God has established. This applies at every level: the authority of establishment institutions — law enforcement, military defense, judicial function, marriage — and the authority of spiritual office within the local church. Arrogance is the great abuser of authority; it either refuses to submit to legitimate authority or exercises authority without accountability.

One practical consequence for the believer is the principle of privacy. Every believer must be allowed the right of self-determination. When a mature believer imposes his doctrinal standards on an immature believer through judgment, maligning, or public correction at the wrong moment, he does precisely what Moses did at Meribah: he distracts from the integrity of God and makes himself the issue. Flexibility toward other believers — recognizing that their areas of weakness are different from one's own — is a function of the royal family honor code. The failure of this flexibility is not a minor social failing; it is a theological error that obscures the foundational issue of logistical grace.

III. Self-Righteousness: Its Nature, Forms, and Consequences

The second clause of Romans 10:3 — 'seeking to establish their own righteousness' — identifies the mechanism of Israel's failure and simultaneously identifies the mechanism by which believers in any generation undermine the grace pipeline. Self-righteousness is the attempt to construct, through human volition and human effort, a righteousness that can stand before God or compel divine blessing. It is, by definition, both arrogance and blasphemy.

A. The Conflict Between Imputed and Self-Produced Righteousness

For the Jewish unbeliever, self-righteousness took the form of law-keeping, ritual observance, and moral conformity pursued as the basis of standing before God. The law offered them God's perfect righteousness through faith in the coming Messiah; they substituted their own performance for His provision. The result was that when the righteousness of God was presented to them in the person and work of Jesus Christ, they refused it — because they already had, in their own estimation, something adequate.

For the born-again believer, the conflict takes a different form. The believer at salvation receives the imputed righteousness of God — an infinite, perfect righteousness that no human production can approach or compete with. The inner conflict that subsequently arises is not a conflict between two equally matched opponents. It is the conflict between the absolute and the fraudulent: between the righteousness of God residing in the believer and the self-righteousness constructed by the old sin nature operating through the arrogance complex.

B. Legitimate Works Distorted into Self-Righteousness

Self-righteousness does not always announce itself as such. One of its most common forms is the distortion of legitimate Christian function into a system of merit. Giving to the local church is a legitimate function. Witnessing is a legitimate function. Prayer is a legitimate function. Teaching, service, and financial stewardship are all legitimate. The distortion occurs when the believer attaches to these activities the expectation that God will bless him because he performed them. At that point, a legitimate work has been converted into a system of self-righteousness, and the believer is building on sand.

God provides the opportunity for witnessing; the integrity of God is the issue. God provides circumstances for prayer; the integrity of God is the issue. God provides financial prosperity that enables giving; the integrity of God is the issue. When the believer performs these functions while keeping the integrity of God as the issue — not what he is doing, but Whose policy is being honored — the function is legitimate and spiritually profitable. When the believer shifts the emphasis to what he himself is doing, the same function becomes self-righteousness, and no divine blessing attaches to it.

C. Morality Without Divine Righteousness

There is a place for morality in the Christian life, but never as a system of self-righteousness. Moral behavior that flows from the possession of divine righteousness and from the filling of the Holy Spirit is legitimate and honoring to God. Moral behavior deployed as the basis of a claim upon God — or as the basis of contempt toward less moral believers — is self-righteousness in one of its most entrenched forms. The morally self-righteous believer becomes critical, inflexible, and incapable of functioning within the privacy framework of the royal family honor code. Ironically, such a believer, regardless of the high quality of his moral production, is operating in arrogance — the very sin that makes the old sin nature most dangerous.

IV. Submission to Divine Righteousness: The Path of Grace

The positive counterpart to self-righteousness is submission — hupotassō — to the righteousness of God. There is only one way to achieve this submission: it begins with faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, by which the righteousness of God is imputed. It continues with the daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), by which the believer learns to think in categories consistent with the grace policy of God. And it culminates in the cracking of the maturity barrier, by which the believer becomes the recipient of supergrace blessing.

Abraham is the pattern. He was a Sumerian-Akkadian Gentile, the product of a polytheistic culture, with no prior claim upon the God of Israel. He believed, and his faith was imputed to him for righteousness. From that moment, God committed to sustaining him through logistical grace — not because Abraham was in any way exceptional as a person, but because Abraham now possessed the righteousness of God and God's integrity demanded provision. Abraham used his freedom to build on that foundation. He advanced through sustained positive volition toward divine revelation. He cracked the maturity barrier — the moment of his circumcision marking the transformation from Gentile Abram to Jewish Abraham, the father of a new race founded on imputed divine righteousness. The Jewish race itself was born out of the implications of that imputation.

The promise of Philippians 4:19 — 'My God shall supply all your need according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus' — is a logistical grace promise. It contains no condition relating to the believer's spiritual state or moral performance. The issue is not whether the believer has behaved well enough to deserve provision. The issue is that the believer possesses divine righteousness, and the integrity of God cannot deny its own righteousness. The same principle underlies Psalm 55:22: 'Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken.' And 1 Peter 5:7: 'Casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.' These are not promises conditioned on merit. They are expressions of the integrity of God.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Four

1. Submission to the righteousness of God begins with faith in Christ. At the moment of belief, the justice of God imputes divine righteousness to the believer on a non-meritorious basis. Faith is non-meritorious — the merit resides in the object, Jesus Christ, not in the act of believing. This imputed righteousness is the foundation of the entire grace pipeline.

2. The integrity of God is the sole issue in logistical grace. God does not sustain believers because they are good, because they have followed a procedure of self-righteousness, or because they have performed acceptable works. He sustains them because they possess His righteousness and He cannot deny it. This applies equally to the reversionist and the mature believer.

3. Logistical grace and supergrace blessing operate on different principles. Logistical blessing is unconditional with respect to spiritual status — all believers receive it by virtue of possessing divine righteousness. Supergrace blessing is conditional upon spiritual advance — it is imputed to the righteousness of God in the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier through sustained doctrine intake.

4. The Second Meribah incident illustrates the danger of obscuring the integrity of God. Moses, a mature believer, failed to make divine integrity the public issue when the congregation required water. By addressing the people in anger and emphasizing human instrumentality, he diverted attention from the grace principle that should have governed the moment. The discipline — forfeiture of the privilege of leading Israel into the land — was proportionate to the magnitude of the failure.

5. Hupotassō is a military term denoting the discipline of occupying one's assigned position under authority. Applied to divine righteousness, it means acknowledging that one's standing before God is determined entirely by the righteousness God has imputed, not by anything the believer produces. Failure to maintain this orientation is the root of both legalism and reversionism.

6. Self-righteousness is both arrogance and blasphemy. It is arrogance because it places human production in competition with divine perfection. It is blasphemy because it denies the grace policy by which God operates — which is the imputation of blessing to His own righteousness, not to human merit. Both the unbeliever's rejection of imputed righteousness and the believer's construction of a competing self-righteousness fall under this indictment.

7. Legitimate works become self-righteousness when they are offered as a basis for divine blessing. Giving, witnessing, prayer, teaching, and service are legitimate Christian functions. When the believer performs them while expecting God to bless him in return, he has distorted a legitimate function into a system of self-righteousness. When he performs them as a response to divine integrity and grace — keeping the integrity of God as the issue rather than his own performance — they are spiritually valid.

8. There is a place for morality in the Christian life, but never as a system of self-righteousness. Moral behavior flowing from the possession of divine righteousness is legitimate. Moral behavior deployed as a basis of merit before God, or as the basis of contempt toward other believers, is self-righteousness in one of its most entrenched forms and constitutes a failure of the royal family honor code.

9. Authority orientation is the practical expression of submission to divine righteousness. The military background of hupotassō connects doctrinal submission to the broader category of authority orientation. The believer who refuses to submit to divinely established authorities — spiritual, governmental, familial — is operating in the same arrogance pattern as Israel refusing to submit to the righteousness of God.

10. Flexibility toward other believers is a theological obligation, not merely a social courtesy. The believer who imposes his doctrinal standards on others through judgment, maligning, or unsolicited correction at the wrong moment obscures the integrity of God in exactly the way Moses did at Meribah. Every believer must be allowed the right of self-determination. This is a function of the royal family honor code and is inseparable from the logistical grace principle.

11. Self-righteousness glorifies the individual; imputed righteousness can only glorify God. Divine righteousness, by its nature, draws all attention to the source — the justice and integrity of God. Self-righteousness, by its nature, draws attention to the human producer. The two systems are therefore incompatible, and the believer who pursues self-righteousness forfeits the capacity to glorify God in time and risks the loss of eternal rewards, though not of salvation.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — the righteousness of God The central subject of Romans. God's own perfect righteousness, imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ on a non-meritorious basis. The organizing axis of the adjustment to the justice of God.
hupotassō ὑποτάσσω hupotassō — to be subordinate, to submit to authority A military compound verb: hupo (under) + tassō (to arrange, to assign a position). Denotes the discipline of occupying one's assigned place within a command structure. Applied in Romans 10:3 to the act of submitting to the authority of God's imputed righteousness. The passive voice indicates the result of a choice: Israel refused to be placed under that authority.
epignosis ἐπίγνωσις epignosis — full, exact knowledge The category of knowledge required for spiritual growth and authority orientation. Distinguished from gnosis (general awareness) by its precision and completeness. Israel's ignorance of the righteousness of God in Romans 10:3 is a failure of epignosis, not of mere information exposure.
logistical grace The provision by God of all that is necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued life on earth. Unconditional with respect to spiritual status — all believers receive it by virtue of possessing divine righteousness. The issue in logistical grace is always the integrity of God, not the merit of the recipient.
GAP Grace Apparatus for Perception The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, processes, and internalizes Bible doctrine. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit, a prepared communicator, and positive volition on the part of the recipient. The daily function of GAP is the mechanism by which logistical grace is translated into the advance toward the maturity barrier.
maturity barrier The threshold of spiritual maturity cracked through sustained intake and application of Bible doctrine over time. The believer who cracks the maturity barrier enters supergrace and becomes eligible for the six categories of special divine blessing. Abraham's circumcision is the pattern: a Gentile who advanced to the point of becoming the father of a new race.
supergrace The stage of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier, characterized by the imputation of six categories of special divine blessing to the righteousness of God in the mature believer. Distinguished from logistical grace in that the believer's spiritual status quo is the issue, not merely the possession of imputed righteousness.
old sin nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line. The source of self-righteousness, arrogance, and all forms of human good that compete with divine righteousness. The old sin nature is not eradicated at salvation but is countered by the filling of the Holy Spirit and the intake of doctrine.
reversionism Retroactive spiritual regression — the process by which a believer abandons positive volition toward doctrine and returns to the thinking and values of the old sin nature. Reversionists still receive logistical grace support because the issue is the integrity of God, but they forfeit supergrace blessing and accumulate divine discipline, which in its terminal form is the sin unto death.

Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five

Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness

Romans 10:4 “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness to each one because he believes.

Romans 10:4 concludes the doctrinal argument opened in verses 1–3, where Paul diagnosed Israel's failure: zeal for God without knowledge of doctrine, resulting in the pursuit of self-righteousness at the expense of God's imputed righteousness. Verse 4 now identifies the definitive theological reason for that failure and its resolution: the person and work of Christ terminates the law as a mechanism of righteousness, because at the moment of faith the believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness. This chapter provides the full grammatical, lexical, and doctrinal analysis of verse 4, together with its place in the plan of God.

I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:4

The Post-Positive Conjunction gar

The sentence opens in Greek with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), rendered in English at the head of the clause as for. As a post-positive conjunction, gar introduces the cause or reason for the preceding statement. Its function here is to ground verse 4 in the argument of verses 1–3: Israel's failure to submit to God's righteousness (v. 3) is explained by the fact that Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness.

The Subject: Christos

The subject is Christos (Χριστός), nominative singular, the fourth word in the Greek word order. The absence of the definite article before Christos is significant: it is qualitative, emphasizing the unique nature of the person rather than mere identification. The anarthrous construction underscores the hypostatic union — the Lord Jesus Christ is eternal God, co-equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and simultaneously true humanity, the last Adam, impeccable, without an old sin nature, without the imputation of Adam's sin, and without personal sin.

The Predicate Nominative: Telos

The verb is supplied by legitimate ellipsis: the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί), the verb of being, which governs two nominative-case nouns and so takes no expressed form. The predicate nominative is telos (τέλος), a neuter noun with the following semantic range in Koine Greek:

In Koine Greek, telos denotes: (1) termination, cessation, end; (2) objective or goal; (3) completion of a state — the final step or supreme stage. In classical Attic usage (notably Demosthenes) it could also carry the sense of obligation or achievement, but these connotations do not carry over into the Koine of the New Testament period. Accordingly, two primary translations are grammatically and lexically admissible in this verse: (a) objective / goal, and (b) termination / cessation.

Contextual considerations — particularly the supporting passages examined below (Romans 3:20, 28; Galatians 2:16; 3:24) — establish that the dominant meaning here is termination or cessation. Christ is the end, the cessation, the termination of the law.

The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices

The noun nomos (νόμος), used here without the definite article, refers to the Mosaic law. Paul elsewhere uses nomos for other portions of Scripture and occasionally for the entire Old Testament canon, but context here specifies the Mosaic law as the system Israel had been attempting to employ for salvation. The Mosaic law comprises three codices:

Codex 1 — The Decalogue. The Ten Commandments define freedom under divine establishment in negative terms (prohibitions), and in so doing they define sin. Hundreds of statements throughout Codex 1 and Codex 3 address hamartiology — mental attitude sins, sins of the tongue, and overt sins — bringing a consciousness of sin (Romans 3:20).

Codex 2 — The Levitical Ordinances. This codex presents a complete Christology and soteriology through typology: the tabernacle and its sacred furniture, the Levitical priesthood and its modus operandi, and the entire sacrificial system all point forward to the Lord Jesus Christ as the only Savior. It is Codex 2 that was fulfilled by the first advent.

Codex 3 — The Laws of Divine Establishment. These govern national life: legitimate government and its limitations, a proportional income tax (ten percent across the board, applicable to believers and unbelievers alike), military function and the draft, dietary regulations, criminal jurisprudence including the requirement of legitimate witnesses and the exclusion of hearsay, and the full range of social relationships.

In this verse, Paul focuses specifically on the law as it bears on righteousness and salvation. Codex 1 and Codex 3 demonstrate that man is a sinner who needs a Savior. Codex 2 reveals that Christ is the only Savior. Keeping any of these codices as a mechanism of salvation produces only self-righteousness; understanding Codex 2 and believing in Christ produces the imputation of divine righteousness.

The Prepositional Phrase: eis dikaiosynēn

The prepositional phrase is eis dikaiosynēn (εἰς δικαιοσύνην). The preposition eis with the accusative expresses reference or respect: with reference to righteousness. The noun dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη) is accusative singular. Paul's specification of this prepositional phrase is deliberate: Christ is the termination of the law not in every conceivable sense, but specifically with reference to righteousness — that is, with respect to the question of how a person obtains standing before God. The phrase eliminates the law as a means of producing righteousness acceptable to God.

The Dative Participle: to pisteuonti

The concluding clause employs the articular present active participle from pisteuō (πιστεύω), dative singular. The dative is a dative of advantage and indirect object from the adjective pas (πᾶς), used as a substantive in the singular: to each one. The definite article functions as a personal pronoun. The present tense is aoristic — punctiliar action at the moment of gospel hearing. The active voice indicates that the individual, at the point of hearing the gospel, produces the action: he believes. The participle is causal.

Corrected translation of the full verse: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness to each one because he believes.

II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages

Several passages confirm that telos here carries the meaning of termination or cessation and illumine the doctrinal content of verse 4.

Romans 3:20 “For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Therefore by the works of the law no human being shall be justified in his presence; for through the law is the consciousness of sin.
Romans 3:28 “For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: We conclude then that man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.
Galatians 2:16 “Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Christ Jesus in order that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, for by the works of the law no human being will be justified.
Galatians 3:24 “So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Therefore the law has become a pedagogue to lead us to Christ that we might be justified by means of faith.

The word rendered guardian or schoolmaster is paidagōgos (παιδαγωγός), the Greek term for a slave who served as a bodyguard-escort for children, accompanying them to and from school to prevent kidnapping or harm. The paidagōgos was not a teacher but a conductor leading the child to the teacher. The Mosaic law functioned in an analogous way: Codex 1 exposed sin and the need for a Savior; Codex 2 revealed Christ as that Savior. The law conducted Israel toward Christ.

Matthew 5:17 — 'Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them' — is not directly pertinent to verse 4. The phrase 'the Law and the Prophets' designates the entire Old Testament canon (the Pentateuch and the Prophetical writings), not the Mosaic law specifically as a mechanism of righteousness. The fulfillment spoken of in Matthew 5:17 is broader in scope than the termination of Codex 2 addressed in Romans 10:4.

III. Christ as Termination of the Law: Two Dimensions

A. Fulfillment of Codex 2 at the First Advent

The first dimension in which Christ is the termination of the law concerns the fulfillment of Codex 2. Every Levitical sacrifice, every holy day, every article of the tabernacle furniture, every procedural function of the Levitical priesthood was a type pointing forward to the person and work of the Lord Jesus Christ. At the first advent, Christ received the imputation of every personal sin of the entire human race and was judged for them in His spiritual death on the cross. His physical death, burial, resurrection, and ascension completed this fulfillment. With the completion of the cross-work, every shadow in Codex 2 found its substance. There is nothing left to fulfill. Codex 2 is terminated.

Israel, however, was blind to the first advent. Rather than receiving the substance to which all the types pointed, Israel retained the shadows and pursued works-righteousness derived from keeping the law. Their self-righteousness stood in direct opposition to the imputed righteousness available through faith in the very Messiah their own law had been advertising.

B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition

The second dimension is dispensational. When Christ ascended and was seated at the right hand of the Father, His session inaugurated a new royal category. The Lord Jesus Christ acquired a new title of royalty that required a royal family, and so the age of Israel was interrupted — not terminated permanently, but suspended. The Church Age is the period in which that royal family is being assembled. At salvation every believer in this dispensation receives thirty-six things simultaneously, one of which is the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which enters the believer into union with Christ seated at the right hand of the Father and constitutes him royal family of God.

During the Church Age — the times of the Gentiles — no Jewish national entity functions as a client nation to God. Only Gentile nations can occupy that role in the present dispensation. When the royal family is complete it will be removed at the resurrection of the Church (the Rapture), the age of Israel will resume, the tribulation will run its course, and at the Second Advent Israel will be restored to client nation status and the four unconditional covenants to Israel will be fulfilled.

In this dispensational sense, Christ is the cessation of the law: the law as the governing economy for God's client nation Israel has been suspended for the duration of the Church Age.

IV. Righteousness, Justification, and the Plan of God

A. The Flow of Divine Blessing Through the Justice of God

All blessing from God to man flows through the justice of God, not directly through His love, sovereignty, or omnipotence. This is the central axis of the Epistle to the Romans. Divine justice must have a target — a home — into which it can impute blessing without compromising the holiness of God. The integrity of God consists of two attributes in union: righteousness and justice. What righteousness demands, justice executes. At the moment of faith in Christ, the justice of God imputes divine righteousness to the believer, establishing in the believer a permanent target for all subsequent divine blessing.

This is why the imputation of divine righteousness is not merely a juridical formality but the structural foundation of the entire Christian life. Without it, God could not bless sinful man without self-contradiction. With it, every category of blessing — logistical grace provision and the special blessings of maturity — flows legitimately from the justice of God to His own righteousness resident in the believer. Not one category of divine blessing ever goes to human self-righteousness.

B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points

The plan of God for every person can be charted across three reference points:

Point X (Physical Birth): The plan of God begins not at the new birth but at physical birth. Human life is imputed to the soul immediately at birth — a real imputation, God personally bestowing life, implying that God has a plan for that individual from the first moment of existence. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed as a real imputation to its genetically-formed home: the old sin nature. This judicial imputation constitutes condemnation. No person is condemned on the basis of personal sins; condemnation rests on the imputation of Adam's sin. The significance is twofold: (1) condemnation must precede salvation, and therefore those who never reach the age of accountability — infants, those with severe cognitive disabilities — are automatically saved through the operation of divine justice; (2) the basis of condemnation is never personal sinful acts, a fact that eliminates arrogant testimonies grounded in false doctrine. When Scripture states 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23, aorist tense), the reference is to the imputation of Adam's sin, not to accumulated personal transgressions. Condemnation at Point X creates the potential of salvation for the entire human race.

Point Y (Salvation): The gospel — pertinent doctrine presenting redemption, reconciliation, and propitiation — constitutes the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. At the moment of faith, salvation adjustment to the justice of God occurs. This involves two judicial imputations: (1) all personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there — they were reserved for the cross, not condemned at birth; (2) the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer, resulting in instant justification. This is the location in the plan of God addressed by Romans 10:4. Christ is the termination of the law with reference to this righteousness imputed at the moment of faith.

Point Z (Spiritual Maturity): The imputation of divine righteousness at Point Y creates a second potential: the imputation of special blessing at maturity. Pertinent doctrine — the daily intake and perception of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception — constitutes the second hope: absolute confidence that sustained doctrine intake over time will crack the maturity barrier and bring the believer to supergrace, at which point the justice of God begins imputing special blessing in six categories to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. This constitutes maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The mature believer at Point Z then possesses the third potential: at the judgment seat of Christ following the Rapture, the imputation of eternal reward and blessing glorifies God permanently. This is the 'all things working together for good' of Romans 8:28 — the agathos, the intrinsic good of the eternal state.

C. Logistical Grace and Special Blessing

Prior to reaching the maturity barrier, all blessing is logistical grace: everything necessary for physical existence and the opportunity to advance spiritually — food, shelter, clothing, freedom, time, access to doctrine, someone to communicate it, transportation, environment. These provisions are imputed from the justice of God to the righteousness of God without any relationship to human merit. The believer does not earn or deserve logistical grace; it flows on the basis of divine integrity alone. This eliminates any system that teaches that giving money to a religious organization produces divine blessing. Tithing in the Old Testament was a ten-percent income tax on all inhabitants of Israel — believers and unbelievers alike — directed to the government treasury, not to a religious organization. It carried no spiritual connotation and was not a mechanism for obtaining divine blessing. Any system that conditions God's blessing on financial giving to a local institution has constructed a self-righteousness framework that competes with imputed divine righteousness, and where that competition exists, grace has been replaced by works.

Special blessings beyond logistical grace — imputed at maturity in six categories — go equally and exclusively to the righteousness of God in the believer. Blessing by association (category three of special blessing) explains the prosperity sometimes observed among unbelievers who are closely associated with mature believers; this is a derivative, not a direct imputation.

V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness

The entire argument of Romans 10:1–4 is the conflict between two systems of righteousness: (1) human self-righteousness generated by keeping the Mosaic law, and (2) divine righteousness imputed at the moment of faith in Christ. These two systems are mutually exclusive. They cannot coexist as complementary approaches to obtaining divine blessing. Either the believer accepts imputed divine righteousness as the sole basis of his standing before God, or he attempts to supplement or replace it with self-generated righteousness. The latter course is legalism, and legalism is defined in this passage as a failure to understand the implications of verse 4.

The Jews Paul addresses here are a specific illustration of a broader pattern. Like the rich young ruler who came to our Lord asking what further deed was required for eternal life — and who acknowledged that he had kept the commandments — they had pursued moral achievement as the currency of salvation. The Lord's response in that encounter confirmed the outward observance while identifying the missing element: personal faith in the one standing before him. No amount of legal compliance can produce the righteousness God requires, because the righteousness God requires is His own — and it is given, not earned.

After salvation the same dynamic applies. Believers who create internal systems of morality, rule-keeping, or religious performance as the basis of their spiritual standing before God have entered into reversionism. They lose momentum. They lose motivation. They substitute human achievement — whether on a witnessing program, a prayer schedule, a morality framework, or any other function — for the genuine advance that comes through the daily perception of doctrine. Their arrogance consists in the assumption that self-achievement can impress God. God is impressed only with His own integrity. His own righteousness is the target; nothing else qualifies.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five

1. Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness. The Greek telos (τέλος) in Romans 10:4 carries the meaning of cessation or termination in this context, confirmed by Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 2:16. Christ is the end of any law-based system for obtaining righteousness before God.

2. Faith in Christ is obedience to the righteousness of God. Romans 10:3 establishes the negative: Israel's failure to be obedient to the righteousness of God. Romans 10:4 supplies the positive: the one who believes in Christ has obeyed the righteousness of God, because believing is the non-meritorious means through which divine righteousness is received.

3. The Jews sought to establish their own righteousness by keeping the law, but Christ is the termination of that system. For all who believe, Christ ends the pursuit of self-righteousness through law-keeping as a means of obtaining divine approval. The first advent fulfilled Codex 2 of the Mosaic law; there is no further typological function for the Levitical system to perform.

4. Christ is the termination of any system of human self-righteousness with respect to righteousness before God. Faith in Christ results in the imputation of God's perfect righteousness. Once that imputation has occurred, no system of human self-righteousness can compete with it. Where the attempt to compete exists, the believer has abandoned grace orientation.

5. No system of human righteousness can compete with God's righteousness. Matthew 6:33 — 'Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness' — presupposes that the believer already possesses imputed divine righteousness as the basis of logistical grace provision. All the things that are 'added' flow to that righteousness, not to any human achievement.

6. Israel failed as a client nation when it substituted self-righteousness for imputed righteousness. The blindness of Israel was the blindness of arrogance — the assumption that self-achievement could impress God. This substitution constituted a stumbling block in the previous dispensation and serves as a warning to Church Age believers against the same error.

7. In the conflict between self-righteousness and divine imputed righteousness, there is no contest. Human arrogance alone concludes that righteousness derived from law-keeping could provide salvation or divine blessing. God's plan of grace not only excludes human self-righteousness but replaces it with His own perfect righteousness, against which no human alternative can compete.

8. The imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith is the foundation and perpetual motivation for advancing to maturity. Because the individual believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation, this constitutes both instant justification and the permanent structural basis for momentum toward spiritual maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

9. The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed righteousness is terminated at salvation when faith in Christ occurs — and must be kept there. The practical application of verse 4 is the refusal to construct any system of self-righteousness that competes with God's imputed righteousness after salvation. Legalism is the arrogance of ignorance: a failure to understand what happened at the moment of faith.

10. Two systems of righteousness are mutually exclusive: self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness. No believer can simultaneously build on both. Christian legalism is the arrogance of seeking to supplement imputed righteousness with self-generated works. Grace orientation is the humble recognition that the foundation is already laid by God and that the building material is the perception of doctrine, not moral performance.

11. The power of thought exceeds the power of deed. Deeds have merit only as they express the thought that motivates them. Bible doctrine resident in the soul is the thought that motivates genuine compliance with the plan of God and produces authentic grace orientation to all of life.

12. Grace excludes any system of self-righteousness as the basis of merit or blessing from God. The only permissible foundation for the Christian life is imputed righteousness, and the only permissible building material is the daily perception of Bible doctrine. Every category of divine blessing — logistical grace and special blessing alike — flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer, never to any form of human self-righteousness.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
telos τέλος telos — end, termination, cessation, goal Neuter noun, Koine Greek. Semantic range includes: termination or cessation; objective or goal; completion of a state; the final or supreme stage. In Romans 10:4, contextual and grammatical evidence supports the meaning termination or cessation, indicating that Christ ends the law as a mechanism for obtaining righteousness before God.
nomos νόμος nomos — law Masculine noun, Koine Greek. Used in the New Testament for the Mosaic law (most frequently), portions of the Old Testament canon, and occasionally the entire canon. In Romans 10:4, nomos refers specifically to the Mosaic law in its three codices: the Decalogue (Codex 1), the Levitical ordinances (Codex 2), and the laws of divine establishment (Codex 3).
dikaiosynē δικαιοσύνη dikaiosynē — righteousness Feminine noun, Koine Greek. The righteousness of God (dikaiosynē theou) is the central doctrinal axis of the Epistle to the Romans. At salvation, God's own perfect righteousness is imputed to the believer, establishing a permanent target in the believer into which the justice of God can impute all categories of divine blessing without compromising divine integrity.
pisteuō πιστεύω pisteuō — to believe, to have faith in Verb, Koine Greek. The basic New Testament word for saving faith. Non-meritorious in nature: the merit resides in the object of faith (Christ), not in the act of believing. In Romans 10:4 the articular present active participle (causal) conveys: because he believes — the faith-act that triggers the imputation of divine righteousness.
gar γάρ gar — for, because Post-positive conjunctive particle, Koine Greek. Introduces a cause or reason for the preceding statement. In Romans 10:4 it connects the verse to the diagnosis of verses 1–3, providing the theological explanation for Israel's failure to submit to God's righteousness.
paidagōgos παιδαγωγός paidagōgos — pedagogue, guardian-escort Masculine noun, Koine Greek. In the Greco-Roman world, the paidagōgos was not a teacher but a trusted slave who escorted children to and from school, providing protection against kidnapping or harm. Paul employs the term in Galatians 3:24 to describe the function of the Mosaic law: it conducted Israel toward Christ (the teacher), not as a method of salvation but as a guide pointing to the only Savior.
eimi εἰμί eimi — to be Verb of being, Koine Greek. Supplied by ellipsis in Romans 10:4 because the words following the subject are in the nominative case (the verb 'to be' governs a predicate nominative). The ellipsis is grammatically legitimate and standard in Greek prose.
pas πᾶς pas — all, every, each Adjective, Koine Greek. Used as a substantive in the dative singular in Romans 10:4, yielding the meaning to each one — a dative of advantage and indirect object emphasizing individual application: the imputation of divine righteousness occurs for each individual believer at the moment of personal faith.
hypostatic union The union of full, undiminished deity and true, complete humanity in the one person of Jesus Christ. The anarthrous use of Christos in Romans 10:4 is qualitative, emphasizing this unique personal constitution. Christ is co-equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit as eternal God and simultaneously the last Adam as true humanity — impeccable, without an old sin nature, without the imputation of Adam's sin, and without personal sin.
logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and opportunity to advance spiritually: food, shelter, clothing, freedom, time, access to doctrine, transportation, environment. Imputed from the justice of God to the righteousness of God without any relationship to human merit. Logistical grace sustains the believer from salvation to physical death.
adjustment to the justice of God The mechanism by which all divine blessing is received. Three categories: (1) salvation adjustment — faith in Christ at the moment of gospel hearing, non-meritorious, once and for all; (2) rebound adjustment — naming known sins to God, restoring fellowship instantly (1 John 1:9), repeated as needed; (3) maturity adjustment — progressive, through daily intake of Bible doctrine over time, culminating in supergrace and ultra-supergrace and the imputation of special blessing.

Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six

Romans 10:4 — Self-Righteousness versus Imputed Divine Righteousness; The Termination of the Law; Four Principles

Romans 10:4 “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness to each one because he believes.

Romans 10:4 stands at the intersection of Israel's failure and the universal principle that all righteousness before God must be received, not achieved. The verse culminates Paul's analysis of Israel's zeal without doctrine (10:1–3) and introduces a four-part doctrinal development grounded in Old Testament documentation from Moses. This chapter completes the exegesis of verse 4 by drawing out the four principles embedded in the verse itself, each of which exposes a dimension of the conflict between human self-righteousness and the imputed divine righteousness that comes through faith in Christ.

I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God

The preceding verse (10:3) established that Israel, not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, failed to be obedient to the righteousness of God. Verse 4 supplies the explanation: obedience to the righteousness of God means faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. It is at the moment of that faith that the integrity of God becomes operative in relation to the believer's life.

The structure of divine integrity is central here. God possesses two attributes that together constitute His holiness: righteousness and justice. At salvation, the justice of God imputes perfect divine righteousness to the believer, establishing what may be called a home or target for all subsequent blessing. All blessing — whether logistical in the maintenance of daily life or special in the reward of spiritual maturity — flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. This pipeline is insulated by grace against any intrusion of human ability, merit, talent, or works.

Grace, properly defined, is the policy of the justice of God in imputing blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. The Greek term charis (χάρις) carries this technical force throughout Paul's argument. Because no human effort can enter this pipeline, the integrity of God is never compromised. Justice cannot bless sinful man directly; it must bless divine righteousness already imputed to man.

The practical consequence is that every competing system — prayer treated as a merit mechanism, giving as a basis for blessing, witnessing as a claim on divine reward, moral achievement, self-sacrifice, or any form of religious performance — is excluded. These activities may be legitimate in their proper context, but they become distortions the moment they are set up as the ground of blessing from God. God does not bless on the basis of what any person does. He blesses on the basis of His own righteousness imputed to the believer and the justice that executes that imputation.

1. Obedience to the righteousness of God is defined as faith in the Lord Jesus Christ: it is at the moment of faith that the justice of God imputes divine righteousness, establishing the target for all blessing.

2. Faith in Christ is obedience to the righteousness of God: no other act, discipline, or sacrifice qualifies as obedience in the soteriological sense.

3. The Jews sought salvation through law-keeping: Christ is the termination of that system, exposing it as a myth incompatible with righteousness by faith.

4. Christ terminates every system of human self-righteousness: faith in Christ results in the imputation of God's perfect righteousness, which no human system can replicate or improve upon.

5. No system of human righteousness can compete with the righteousness of God: Matthew 6:33 directs the believer to seek the kingdom and His righteousness first, with logistical blessing following as the consequence.

6. Israel as client nation failed by substituting law-righteousness for faith-righteousness: the rich young ruler is the classic illustration — moral near-perfection in law-keeping produced the assumption of salvation rather than its reality.

7. In the conflict of self-righteousness versus imputed divine righteousness, there is no contest: the arrogance of the believer is the only faculty capable of imagining that human performance could rival the righteousness of God.

8. Only human arrogance concludes that law-keeping provides salvation: this error is as old as the fall and recurs in every dispensation in new forms.

9. God's plan excludes human self-righteousness and provides the solution by His own perfect righteousness: no competition with divine righteousness is possible because it has never failed across all of human and angelic history.

10. The blindness of Israel was the blindness of arrogance: the assumption that self-achievement can impress God is both the root of legalism and a perpetual state of sinning.

11. God is impressed only with His own integrity: no human counterfeit of righteousness — however sincere — registers with divine justice as a basis for blessing.

II. Second Principle: Imputed Righteousness as Justification and Motivation

The imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ accomplishes two things simultaneously: it constitutes instant justification, and it establishes perpetual motivation for the believer's advance to spiritual maturity. The mechanism is traced through the divine plan by means of three paired stages, each consisting of an imputation that creates potential, a doctrinal cognizance that converts potential into hope, and a grace execution that replaces hope with reality.

A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan

The first stage encompasses the pre-salvation condition. At birth, every human being receives two imputations: human life to the soul, and Adam's original sin to the genetically transmitted sin capacity. The second imputation establishes the potential for salvation, since condemnation must precede the offer of deliverance. Gospel doctrine — covering Christ's substitutionary judgment, redemption, reconciliation, propitiation, and justification — converts that potential into hope, defined as absolute confidence about a future certainty. The first hope is the certainty that faith in Christ produces eternal life. This confidence, enabled by the common grace ministry of the Holy Spirit, is replaced by the reality of salvation at the moment of faith — the salvation adjustment to the justice of God through efficacious grace.

The second stage is the believer's life in time. Two judicial imputations anchor this stage: all personal sins were imputed to Christ at the cross, providing the basis for His saving work; and divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at the moment of salvation. This second imputation establishes a new potential — the possibility of great blessing in time that glorifies God. Logistical grace is already a reality from salvation onward. As the believer functions daily in the grace apparatus for perception under the enabling ministry of the Holy Spirit, doctrine accumulates in the soul, and the second hope develops: absolute confidence that maximum doctrine resident in the soul will produce spiritual maturity. That hope is replaced by the reality of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

The third stage encompasses eternity. The imputation of eternal life at salvation, combined with the special blessing imputed to the mature believer in time, establishes a third potential: eternal reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. The third hope is absolute confidence that at the resurrection and evaluation of Church Age believers, eternal reward will be imputed to those who have advanced to maturity. This final imputation glorifies God forever and constitutes the completion of the divine plan.

Throughout all three stages, doctrine is the operative factor. Without knowledge of doctrine there is no motivation for the plan, no momentum within it, and no capacity to receive its blessings. The grace system of perception bypasses human intellectual capacity and establishes a Spirit-enabled system for the reception and internalization of divine truth.

1. Imputed divine righteousness is instant justification and perpetual motivation: it drives the believer's advance to maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

2. The conflict between law-righteousness and faith-righteousness is terminated at salvation: self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness are mutually exclusive systems.

3. Imputed righteousness at salvation displaces any system of self-righteousness or pseudo-spirituality: Christian legalism is the arrogance of ignorance — failure to understand what imputed righteousness already provides.

4. Christian legalism is the arrogance of ignorance: it consists in failing to understand the full implications of what God has already supplied through imputed righteousness.

5. No believer can maintain two conflicting systems of righteousness simultaneously: self-righteousness and divine righteousness are mutually exclusive — one must be abandoned for the other.

6. To establish self-righteousness is the arrogance of legalism: to build on imputed righteousness is the humble grace orientation produced by inculcated doctrine.

7. For the believer, building on imputed righteousness is grace orientation to life: it is the posture produced by doctrine resident in the soul, not by religious performance.

8. The power of thought exceeds the power of deed: the deed possesses merit only insofar as it is the expression of doctrine-based thinking; Christianity is what the believer thinks, not what he performs or professes.

9. Bible doctrine resident in the soul is the thought that motivates compliance with the plan of God: it is the only resource that sustains the believer under pressure, in isolation, and at the approach of death.

10. Grace excludes self-righteousness as any basis for merit or blessing from God: tithing, public works, and religious performance are excluded by the same principle that excludes law-keeping.

11. Building on imputed righteousness requires maximum perception of doctrine: no alternative foundation exists for the Christian life.

12. The conflict of self-righteousness versus divine righteousness existed in the previous dispensation: Israel's stumbling block was adopted wholesale by subsequent religious systems that substituted performance-based religion for faith-righteousness.

III. Third Principle: Imputed Righteousness Replaces Self-Righteousness as the Foundation

Faith in Christ is the end of self-righteousness because it introduces a foundation that human righteousness cannot replicate. Every believer, at the moment of faith, receives the imputed righteousness of God as the permanent base on which the Christian life is constructed. The superstructure built on that foundation consists of Bible doctrine accumulated through the daily function of the grace apparatus for perception. When the superstructure reaches completion in the attainment of spiritual maturity, God imputes special blessing to the building — not because of anything the believer has done, but because the believer now has the capacity to receive blessing without being destroyed by it.

Blessing without capacity intensifies misery rather than producing happiness. Wealth imputed to a believer without the capacity for money produces new and more complex problems. Leadership responsibility given to a believer without the capacity for authority multiplies pressure. The right circumstance of life presented to a believer without the inner resources to sustain it becomes a burden. The solution is never to pursue the blessing; it is to pursue the doctrine that builds the capacity, and to allow the justice of God to execute the imputation at the appropriate time.

1. Faith in Christ is the end of self-righteousness: no human system of holiness can improve on, supplement, or compete with imputed righteousness from God.

2. Imputed righteousness from God resides in every believer: the objective of the Christian life is to ensure that self-righteousness does not simultaneously reside there as a competing system.

3. Christ is the end of every system of human self-righteousness for the believer: baptism, religious experience, self-denial, separation from worldliness, and adherence to taboos are among the recurrent forms this takes.

4. Faith in Christ establishes a new foundation on which the believer builds his life: that foundation is God's righteousness, and the building material is Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

5. Imputed righteousness cannot be improved: the believer's only legitimate activity is to build on the foundation of God's perfect righteousness using the building material of Bible doctrine.

6. When the superstructure of maturity is completed, God imputes special blessing: special blessing requires capacity; capacity requires maximum doctrine resident in the soul through the daily function of the grace apparatus for perception.

7. No system of self-righteousness can receive blessing from the justice of God: giving, sacrifice, and religious performance when presented as merit mechanisms constitute self-righteousness and are excluded from the blessing pipeline.

8. All systems of self-righteousness and pseudo-spirituality have been excluded from the Christian way of life: this includes spirituality by works in any form.

IV. Fourth Principle: The Antiquity of the Conflict and Its Old Testament Documentation

The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness is not a New Testament innovation. It is as old as the fall of man. The first act of human self-righteousness was the manufacture of garments from fig leaves in Genesis 3 — the assumption that a human solution to the problem of nakedness and guilt could constitute adjustment to God. Every subsequent generation has reproduced that assumption in new forms.

Paul does not construct his argument about self-righteousness from New Testament materials alone. He draws on Moses, who addressed this conflict at the inception of Israel's existence as a client nation. Two passages from the Mosaic corpus are brought forward in the verses immediately following, each serving a distinct doctrinal function.

A. Leviticus 18:5 — The Warning against Law-Righteousness (Romans 10:5)

The first Old Testament documentation, cited in Romans 10:5, comes from Leviticus 18:5. Paul uses this text as a warning against depending on righteousness through law-keeping. Moses himself, at the beginning of the dispensation of Israel as a client nation, placed this caveat in the record. The Mosaic law was never intended to function as a mechanism of salvation; its function within Codex 2 — the ordinances — was to reveal the person and work of Jesus Christ, demanding faith in Him as the only Savior.

B. Deuteronomy 30:11–14 — The Importance of Imputed Righteousness (Romans 10:6–8)

The second Old Testament documentation, drawn from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, appears in Romans 10:6–8. This passage emphasizes the importance of building on the foundation of imputed divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ. Together the two Mosaic citations frame the issue: the first warns against the error of law-righteousness; the second commends the reception of righteousness through faith.

C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation

The conclusion of Paul's argument in Romans 10:9–10 will present the pattern of salvation in any dispensation on the basis of cause and result. These verses have been frequently misappropriated as a warrant for public confession as a condition of salvation; the exegesis will demonstrate that they present cause and effect — faith as the internal cause, confession as the external expression of an already-accomplished reality.

The Mosaic law operated through three codices. Codex 1 comprised the Decalogue; Codex 2 comprised the ordinances, which foreshadowed and demanded faith in Jesus Christ as the God of Israel and only Savior; Codex 3 comprised the laws of divine establishment governing social order. The unbelieving Jew bypassed Codex 2, distorted Codex 1 into a pseudo-salvation system, and enlisted Codex 3 for moral self-justification. In the Church Age, the same rejection takes the form of accepting the alpha glory of the God of Israel while blotting out the omega glory — the incarnation, substitutionary death, and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ.

The Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4, Šəmaʿ Yisrāʾēl YHWH ʾĔlōhênû YHWH ʾEḥād (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד), is correctly rendered: 'Jesus Christ is our God; Jesus Christ is unique.' The rejection of this identity — the refusal to recognize the Lord Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of Codex 2 — is the definitive act of unbelief in both dispensations.

1. The conflict of self-righteousness versus imputed righteousness is as old as the fall of man: the first act of human self-righteousness was the manufacture of fig-leaf garments in Genesis 3.

2. This conflict is an Old Testament subject as well as a New Testament subject: Paul is not introducing a novelty but exposing a perennial pattern.

3. Paul develops the conflict as a warning from Moses at the beginning of the dispensation of Israel: the documentation from the Mosaic corpus anchors the argument in Old Testament canonical authority.

4. Romans 10:5 quotes Leviticus 18:5 as a warning against depending on righteousness by law-keeping: Moses himself placed this warning at the inception of the client nation.

5. Romans 10:6–8 quotes Deuteronomy 30:11–14 to emphasize building on the foundation of imputed righteousness: the two Mosaic texts together frame the conflict from both sides — the warning and the commendation.

6. Romans 10:9–10 presents the pattern of salvation in any dispensation on the basis of cause and result: cause is internal faith; result is the external expression of an accomplished reality.

7. Additional meaning in Romans 10:9–10 will be developed in subsequent exegesis: the passage bears more doctrinal content than its popular use as an invitation formula suggests.

8. Codex 2 of the Mosaic law reveals Christ as the only Savior and demands faith in Him: this is the canonical function that the unbelieving Jew systematically bypassed.

9. The unbeliever in the Church Age rejects the first advent of Christ, which fulfills Codex 2: this rejection mirrors the Old Testament pattern of bypassing the ordinances.

10. In both dispensations, the unbelieving Jew rejects imputed righteousness by rejecting Christ as Savior: in the previous dispensation he distorted Codex 1 and 3 into pseudo-salvation; in the current dispensation he blots out the omega glory of the incarnation.

11. The issue in both dispensations is self-righteousness or works-righteousness versus faith-righteousness: imputed righteousness from God, received through faith, is the only righteousness that satisfies divine justice.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six

1. Romans 10:4 defines obedience to the righteousness of God as faith in Christ alone: every other definition of religious obedience is exposed as a form of self-righteousness.

2. The justice-to-righteousness pipeline is insulated by grace against all human intrusion: no work, talent, moral achievement, or religious performance can introduce blessing into a system designed to operate exclusively between the justice of God and the righteousness of God resident in the believer.

3. The three-stage structure of the divine plan — salvation, maturity, and eternal reward — is entirely driven by doctrine: each stage consists of an imputation that creates potential, a doctrinal cognizance that produces hope, and a grace execution that replaces hope with reality.

4. Self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness are mutually exclusive systems: the believer must build exclusively on the foundation of imputed righteousness, using the building material of Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

5. Capacity must precede special blessing: blessing given without capacity intensifies misery; doctrine builds the capacity that makes it possible for justice to impute special blessing without harm.

6. The power of thought exceeds the power of deed: Christianity is what the believer thinks; doctrine resident in the soul is the only resource that sustains the believer under pressure, at the approach of death, or in any condition of isolation from external support.

7. The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed righteousness is as old as the fall: Moses addressed it at the inception of Israel's dispensation, and Paul draws on both Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 30:11–14 as canonical witnesses to the antiquity and universality of the principle.

8. Codex 2 of the Mosaic law was designed to reveal Christ and demand faith in Him: the unbelieving Jew's bypass of Codex 2 is reproduced in the Church Age as the blotting out of the first advent — the rejection of the omega glory of the Lord Jesus Christ.

9. Romans 10:9–10 will present salvation in any dispensation by cause and result: internal faith is the cause; external confession is the result, not an additional condition of salvation.

10. The goal of Bible teaching is to make the believer spiritually self-sustaining: doctrine resident in the soul must function independently in every circumstance of life, because no external resource — human or institutional — can substitute for it when pressure reaches its maximum.

Codex 2 (Mosaic Law) The second section of the Mosaic law, comprising the ordinances (sacrificial system, Levitical ceremonies, and typological institutions). Designed to reveal the person and saving work of Jesus Christ and to demand faith in Him as the God of Israel and only Savior. Bypassed by the unbelieving Jew in favor of Codex 1 (Decalogue) as a pseudo-salvation mechanism.
