The Jews of the second generation had watched Moses disappear above the cloud line on Sinai for forty days. In their irreverence they had drawn the conclusion that Moses had gone to heaven to receive the law; the golden calf incident was the direct consequence. The young people of the next generation repeated this reasoning sarcastically: if salvation is in heaven, who is going to go up and get it for us the way Moses did?

Moses' response is unambiguous: salvation is not in heaven. Therefore it is attainable. Because it is attainable, there is no excuse for substituting human righteousness — law-keeping, morality, self-discipline, religious performance — for the divine righteousness that God imputes to the one who believes in Christ. Morality is not wrong in itself; it functions properly within the divine establishment framework. But morality pressed into service as a means of salvation is not only wrong — it is evil, because it sets human righteousness in competition with the perfect righteousness of God.

Unavailable — Salvation Is Not Across the Sea

The second technical concept is unavailability. Crossing the sea was impossible for Israel: the nation had no navy and no maritime capacity. If salvation were located on the other side of the ocean, it would be practically unavailable regardless of its theoretical existence. Paul, writing after the first century had seen Jewish merchant vessels sailing throughout the Mediterranean world, updates the image from 'across the sea' to 'at the bottom of the sea' — a location even more inaccessible, underscoring the contrast between the extremity of such distance and the actual nearness of salvation.

The double negative structure of the passage is therefore:

Location Technical Status Moses' / Paul's Assertion
Heaven Unattainable Salvation is NOT unattainable — it is not in heaven
Sea / Ocean floor Unavailable Salvation is NOT unavailable — it is not across the sea
Right lobe / Mouth Near Salvation IS near — as close as your soul and your body

The rhythm of the passage is deliberate: heaven and the sea represent the two extremes of inaccessibility — the highest point above and the most remote point at or beneath the surface. Against these extremes, Moses places the right lobe and the mouth — the inward faculty of faith and the outward vehicle of confession. Salvation cannot be closer than one's own soul and one's own body.

V. Deuteronomy 30:12 — Salvation Is Not Unattainable

Deuteronomy 30:12 “It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: It, salvation, is not in heaven, so that you must say: Who will go up to heaven for us, that he might bring it, salvation, to us, and cause us to hear it, so that we might do it?

The subject of the sentence is the pronoun hu (הוּא), meaning it, referring to salvation. The prepositional phrase ba-shamayim (בַּשָּׁמַיִם) means in the heavens. The negative particle lo (לֹא) negates the entire clause: it is not in heaven. Moses then represents the rationalist conclusion that would follow if salvation were in heaven: the people would be compelled to say, who will go up for us?

Two verbs in this clause are particularly significant. The Hiphil stem of shama (שָׁמַע), to hear, produces a causative meaning: to cause to hear, to make hear. The people are imagining a successor to Moses — someone with sufficient authority and genius to compel their attention and subordinate their intelligence. This is arrogance masquerading as discernment: they will not hear unless the teacher is demonstrably their superior. The second significant verb is asah (עָשָׂה), to do. The people want to do something for salvation. Their entire orientation is toward works. Hear it and do it — this is the self-righteous program. Moses exposes the error: you do not do anything for salvation. You believe.

Doctrinal principles from Deuteronomy 30:12:

1. Salvation is not in heaven. Therefore it is attainable.

2. Because salvation is attainable, there is no excuse for substituting human righteousness for divine righteousness.

3. The Hiphil of shama — 'cause to hear' — reveals the arrogance of the second generation: they would not subordinate themselves to any teacher they considered their intellectual inferior.

4. The verb 'do' exposes the works orientation: they intended to do the law for salvation. Paul will demonstrate that Moses himself never taught this.

5. Paul's expansion of this verse in Romans 10:6 adds a crucial Christological dimension: to say that salvation is in heaven is, after the first advent, to say that Christ must be brought down again — a denial of the completed work of the cross.

VI. Paul's Christological Expansion in Romans 10:6

When Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:12 in Romans 10:6, he adds a parenthetical clause not found in Moses: 'that is, to bring Christ down from above.' This expansion is not a departure from Moses but a Christological application that Moses could not make because the first advent had not yet occurred. Paul's argument operates on two levels simultaneously.

First, the historical level: Moses addressed the second generation's arrogant rationalism — their insistence that salvation was inaccessible without a successor to Moses who could ascend to heaven and retrieve it. Moses refuted this by declaring that salvation is not in heaven; it is attainable here and now through faith.

Second, the post-advent level: Paul addresses the blackout of the first-century Jewish community. The Jews of his day recognized the Alpha glory of the God of Israel who appeared to Moses, but they rejected the Omega glory of Christ crucified. Their law-keeping was not simply moralism; it was a denial that the Messiah had already come and completed His work. To insist on salvation by law-keeping after the cross is, in effect, to demand that Christ descend from heaven again — as though His first advent were insufficient. Paul confronts this directly: the first advent has already taken place. Christ has already borne sin on the cross. The work is done. Salvation is not only attainable in principle; it is accomplished in history.

The term 'blackout' refers to the condition of sustained negative volition toward the gospel that produces scar tissue of the soul — a hardened inability to perceive and receive divine truth. In Israel's case this blackout was corporate as well as individual, and it accounts both for the nation's rejection of the Messiah and for the catastrophic consequences Paul describes in Romans 9–11.

VII. The Self-Righteousness of the Second Generation as a Mirror of the Soul

Moses did not write Deuteronomy 30 simply as a historical correction to second-generation Israel. He wrote it for every generation. The failure of the Jews — their rejection of attainable salvation and the substitution of self-righteousness in its place — is a photograph of the soul in every age.

The mechanism of that failure is arrogance. Arrogance is the most basic and most universal function of the old sin nature. It is the root from which self-righteousness grows. The smarter the person, the more subtly arrogance operates; the less acute the intellect, the more obvious its expression. The Jews of the second generation were extraordinarily intelligent, and their self-righteousness was correspondingly sophisticated. They did not say openly that they were rejecting grace; they said that they were honoring Moses. They built a wall of law-keeping against the very gospel that Moses had proclaimed, and then they called the wall piety.

Paul uses this to make a universal point. The principle of adjustment to the justice of God — salvation by faith in Christ — is not a Pauline innovation. It is the teaching of Moses, taught in the full knowledge that the people would reject it in favor of works. Neither Moses nor Paul taught that morality is wrong. What they both taught is that morality cannot accomplish salvation. When human righteousness is offered to God as the grounds for acceptance, it does not merely fall short — it competes with divine righteousness, and that competition is the essence of arrogance.

The wall that arrogance builds against God always collapses under the weight of divine justice. National expressions of this principle include the judgments that fell on Israel repeatedly throughout the Old Testament era. The five cycles of discipline described in Leviticus 26 represent the escalating pressure of divine justice against a nation that has replaced grace with self-righteousness. The same mechanism operates in any client nation in any era. The corrective in every case is the same: salvation is attainable, not by works but by faith; not from heaven, but from the right lobe.

VIII. The Contrast Between Moses and Mosaic Distortion

There is no contradiction between Moses in Deuteronomy and Paul in Romans. Both men wrote under the superintendence of God the Holy Spirit. The contradiction is between what Moses actually wrote and what the tradition of self-righteous interpretation made of it. Moses proclaimed salvation by faith; the rabbinic tradition transformed his law into a meritorious system. Paul does not attack Moses — he defends Moses against his misreaders.

Similarly, there is no contradiction between Codex 1 (establishment law, the Ten Commandments) and Codex 2 (the gospel, the way of salvation). The Ten Commandments were given to guarantee the freedom of the will — to protect the social order in which each person remains free to accept or reject Christ. They were never intended to be the means of earning what only grace can give. When the second generation took the tables of stone that Moses had brought down and elevated them into a soteriology, they did not honor Moses. They inverted him.

Paul's use of the same Mosaic vocabulary — unattainable, unavailable, right lobe, mouth — is deliberate. He speaks to people who revere Moses and despise Paul, and he demonstrates that Paul and Moses are saying exactly the same thing: salvation is near you. It is in your mouth and in your right lobe. It does not require a journey to heaven or across the sea, a system of meritorious observance, or the coming of another Moses. It requires faith.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-One

1. The adversative conjunction de (δέ) in Romans 10:6 establishes a formal contrast between works-righteousness (verse 5, citing Leviticus 18:5) and faith-righteousness. The imputed righteousness of God, received through faith alone, is the subject of what follows.

2. Paul personifies faith-righteousness as a communicating agent, using the retroactive progressive present of legō (λέγω): what Moses wrote in Deuteronomy 30 continues to speak in Paul's day and in every subsequent generation.

3. Verse 11 of Deuteronomy 30 provides the contextual framework: the commandment of salvation is not too difficult and not too far away. These two negatives introduce the technical vocabulary that structures Romans 10:6–8.

4. Two technical terms govern the entire passage: unattainable (salvation is not in heaven) and unavailable (salvation is not across the sea or at the bottom of the ocean). These must not be confused or conflated.

5. Salvation is attainable because it is not in heaven. Therefore, there is no excuse for substituting human righteousness from law-keeping for the divine righteousness that God imputes to the believer.

6. Salvation is available because it is not across the sea. Paul updates Moses' image from 'across the sea' to 'at the bottom of the sea,' intensifying the contrast between remote inaccessibility and the actual nearness of salvation.

7. The Hiphil causative of shama (שָׁמַע) — 'cause to hear' — reveals the second generation's arrogant prerequisite for attention: they would only listen to a teacher demonstrably superior to themselves. This is arrogance operating as intellectual discernment.

8. The verb asah (עָשָׂה) — 'to do' — exposes the works orientation of the second generation: they intended to do the law for salvation. Moses refutes this within the same passage.

9. Paul's parenthetical expansion — 'that is, to bring Christ down from above' — adds a post-advent Christological dimension that Moses could not include. After the first advent, insisting on law-righteousness is equivalent to demanding a second incarnation, as though the cross were insufficient.

10. The Jewish rejection of faith-righteousness in Paul's day is an expression of what the transcript terms the 'blackout' — scar tissue of the soul produced by sustained negative volition toward the gospel — operating at both individual and national levels.

11. There is no contradiction between Moses and Paul. The contradiction is between Moses correctly interpreted and Moses distorted by arrogance and self-righteousness. Paul defends Moses against his misreaders.

12. The principle that morality is not wrong but cannot save applies universally. Human righteousness set against divine righteousness as the grounds for acceptance before God is not merely inadequate — it is the quintessence of arrogance.

13. Salvation is as close as the right lobe and the mouth — as close as the soul and the body. The right lobe is the faculty of faith; the mouth is the vehicle for expressing that faith to God. Nothing could be nearer.

14. Romans 10:9–10 cannot be understood in isolation. The technical framework of attainability and availability established in verses 6–8 — drawn from Deuteronomy 30:12–14 — is the prerequisite for understanding what believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth means.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
de δέ de — but, and, now Greek adversative or continuative conjunction. In Romans 10:6 it functions as a strong adversative, setting faith-righteousness in contrast to law-righteousness introduced in verse 5.
dikaiosynē δικαιοσύνη dikaiosynē — righteousness, justice Noun from dikaios (just, righteous). In Romans 10:6 it refers specifically to the divine righteousness imputed to the believer at the moment of faith in Christ. Contrasted with the human righteousness produced by law-keeping.
pistis πίστις pistis — faith, belief Non-meritorious perception directed toward a legitimate object. In Romans 10:6 the righteousness ek pisteōs (from faith, by means of faith) is the righteousness received entirely apart from human merit or works.
legō λέγω legō — to say, to speak, to communicate Present active indicative in Romans 10:6. Used in the personification of faith-righteousness as a communicating agent. The retroactive progressive present indicates that what Moses wrote in Deuteronomy 30 continues to speak into the present.
houtōs οὕτως houtōs — in this manner, thus, so Adverb of manner in Romans 10:6. Introduces the content of what faith-righteousness communicates, connecting Paul's statement to the quotation from Deuteronomy 30:12.
mitzwah מִצְוָה mitzwah — commandment, precept Hebrew noun, cognate with the verb tsawah (to command). In Deuteronomy 30:11 it refers to the commandment of salvation — the call to believe in the Lord — though the term encompasses all three divisions of the Mosaic law.
tsawah צָוָה tsawah — to command, to charge Hebrew verb from which mitzwah is derived. The cognate construction in Deuteronomy 30:11 ("this commandment which I command you") underscores the authoritative character of the salvation presentation.
shamayim שָּׁמַיִם shamayim — heaven, the heavens Hebrew plural noun. In Deuteronomy 30:12 it identifies the location that salvation does NOT occupy, establishing the technical concept of unattainability: if salvation were in heaven, it would be beyond human reach.
lo לֹא lo — not, no Hebrew negative particle. In Deuteronomy 30:12 it negates the prepositional phrase ba-shamayim: it is not in heaven. This negative is the foundation of the technical term unattainable.
shama (Hiphil) שָׁמַע shama — to hear; Hiphil: to cause to hear Hebrew verb. In the Hiphil causative stem in Deuteronomy 30:12, it means to cause to hear. The second generation demanded a teacher of sufficient authority to compel their attention — revealing an arrogance that conditioned hearing on the perceived superiority of the speaker.
asah עָשָׂה asah — to do, to make, to accomplish Hebrew verb. In Deuteronomy 30:12 the people's stated goal is "that we might do it." This works-orientation — doing the law for salvation — is what Moses is refuting. Faith is non-meritorious perception; it is not doing.
Unattainable Technical term used in the exegesis of Deuteronomy 30:12 and Romans 10:6. Salvation is not in heaven; therefore it is not unattainable. If salvation were unattainable, there would be some justification for substituting human righteousness. Since it is attainable — by faith, here and now — no such justification exists.
Unavailable Technical term used in the exegesis of Deuteronomy 30:13 and Romans 10:7. Salvation is not across the sea or at the bottom of the ocean; therefore it is not unavailable. The distinction between unattainable (vertical: heaven) and unavailable (horizontal: sea) must be maintained throughout the passage.
Blackout of the soul The condition of the right lobe when sustained negative volition toward divine truth has produced scar tissue that cuts off the perception of the gospel. In Romans 9–11, Paul addresses the corporate blackout of Israel with respect to Christ as Messiah — recognition of His Alpha glory as the God of Israel, combined with rejection of His Omega glory as the crucified Savior.
Adjustment to the justice of God δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The central organizing principle of Romans. All divine blessing flows through the justice of God. Salvation adjustment — faith in Christ — is the first and foundational category, in which divine righteousness is imputed to the believer and the claims of justice are permanently satisfied.
Old sin nature (OSN) The sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line. Arrogance is its most basic and universal expression. Self-righteousness — the substitution of human moral achievement for divine righteousness — is arrogance operating in the religious domain.
Client nation A national entity functioning under a covenant relationship with God, charged with the preservation of the canon of Scripture, the support of missionary activity, and the maintenance of a spiritual pivot of mature believers. Israel in the Old Testament era and various Gentile nations in the Church Age have functioned as client nations.

Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Two

Deuteronomy 30:13–14 | Romans 10:6–8 | Salvation: Attainable and Available — Moses, Amos, and Paul

Deuteronomy 30:13–14 “Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Neither is it salvation over the sea or beyond the sea so that you must say, who will cross the sea for us in order that he might bring it — salvation — to us and cause us to hear it, that we might do it. But the word — salvation — is very near to you, in your mouth and in your right lobe, that you may do it — believe in Christ.
Romans 10:6–8 “But the righteousness based on faith says, 'Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?" (that is, to bring Christ down) or "Who will descend into the abyss?" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim).'” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But the righteousness which is by means of faith communicates in this manner: Do not say in your right lobe, who will ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down — or who will descend into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does it say? The word — salvation — is very near you, in your mouth and in your right lobe — that is, the word of faith which we proclaim.

We are in the midst of the extended Old Testament passage in Deuteronomy 30:11–14, which Paul quotes systematically in Romans 10:6–8. Having examined verses 11–12 in previous sessions, this chapter completes the exegesis of verses 13–14 and then addresses in detail the structural question central to Romans 10: why Paul modifies Moses's analogy of the sea with Amos's analogy of Sheol, and what that substitution reveals about the first advent of the Lord Jesus Christ.

I. Deuteronomy 30:13 — Salvation Is Not Unavailable

A. The Hebrew of Verse 13

Verse 13 opens with a prefixed mem combined with a Qal infinitive of the verb עבר (*ʿavar*), yielding the sense "over" or "beyond." The corrected translation: Neither is it salvation over the sea or beyond the sea so that you must say.

The interrogative pronoun mi (מִי) — who — introduces the rhetorical question: who will cross the sea for us? This is followed by the Qal imperfect of ʿavar, to pass over, and then by the Qal perfect of laqach (לָקַח) — to seize and bring — rendered: that he might bring it — salvation — to us.

The final clause, that we may hear it and do it, employs the Hiphil perfect of שָמַע (*shamaʼ*), the causative stem: just as Moses caused Israel to hear the Torah at Sinai under the ministry of the Spirit, so the gospel is caused to be heard. The feminine suffixes throughout match the feminine gender of Torah (*תורה*). Paul, quoting this passage, narrows the referent to Code X2 of the Mosaic Law — the salvation provisions — rather than the whole legal corpus.

The Qal imperfect of ʿasah (עָשָה) — to do — in this context means to believe in Christ, since faith is the doing that Moses commends in Code X2. Corrected translation of verse 13: Neither is it salvation over the sea or beyond the sea so that you must say, who will cross the sea for us in order that he might bring it — salvation — to us and cause us to hear it, that we might do it — believe in Christ.

B. The Theological Point of Verse 13

If verse 12 answers the objection of unattainability (salvation is not in heaven, beyond human reach), verse 13 answers the objection of unavailability: salvation is not geographically remote. Geographical isolation — across a sea, beyond a frontier, in an unreached region — is no barrier to the divine provision of salvation. Wherever positive volition toward God exists, God assumes responsibility to provide the information necessary for a person to respond in faith.

II. Deuteronomy 30:14 — Salvation Is Near

Verse 14 is the conclusion of the unit (vv. 11–14) and the culmination of Moses's argument.

The adversative conjunction ki (כִּי) sets up the contrast: but — instead of being in heaven (unattainable) or across the sea (unavailable), salvation is as near as the believer's own body and soul.

The key noun is dabar (דָּבָר) — word. In this context dabar refers to the doctrine of salvation, the gospel content embedded within Code X2 of the Mosaic Law. Salvation is not written on tablets of stone; it is not locked in a text. It is in the right lobe of every person who has volition and a soul.

In your mouth — the body, the instrument of expression, through which the words of faith are formed even in silent interior speech directed to God. In your heart — the right lobe of the soul, where faith as a non-meritorious system of perception operates. The conclusion: salvation is as near as body and soul. Nothing is closer.

Corrected translation of Deuteronomy 30:14: But the word — salvation through faith in Christ — is very near to you, in your mouth and in your right lobe, that you may do it — believe in Christ.

III. The Structure of Deuteronomy 30:11–14

The four-verse unit is logically organized around a premise and three conclusions.

1. Verse 11 — The Premise: The commandment of faith in Christ (Code X2) is not too difficult (unattainable) and not too far away (unavailable).

2. Verse 12 — First Conclusion: Salvation is not in heaven, where it would be unattainable. Heaven does not need to be scaled.

3. Verse 13 — Second Conclusion: Salvation is not across the sea, where it would be unavailable. No sea needs to be crossed.

4. Verse 14 — Third Conclusion: Salvation is as near as mouth and heart — body and soul. It is attainable and available to every person.

IV. Paul's Use of Deuteronomy 30 in Romans 10:6–8

A. The Correspondence of Citations

Paul quotes the Deuteronomy passage in three stages, each corresponding to one verse of Moses's argument:

• Romans 10:6 quotes Deuteronomy 30:12 (heaven — unattainable), adding the implication of the first advent: that is, to bring Christ down from heaven.• Romans 10:7 quotes Deuteronomy 30:13 in principle (unavailable), but changes the illustration from across the sea to the abyss — Sheol.• Romans 10:8 quotes Deuteronomy 30:14 exactly (salvation is near), preparing the reader for the correct interpretation of Romans 10:9–10.

B. Why Paul Changes the Sea Analogy to Sheol

The critical exegetical question of this section is this: Moses uses the sea as his illustration of unavailability. Paul replaces it with Sheol. Why?

The answer requires three observations working together: the historical situation of the first advent, the passage in Amos 9:2, and the anatomy of what happened to the humanity of Christ at physical death.

C. Amos 9:2 and the Substitution of Sheol for the Sea

Amos 9:2 reads: Though they dig into Sheol, from there shall my hand take them; and though they ascend into heaven, from there I will bring them down. This verse provides Paul with an Old Testament precedent that pairs heaven with Sheol as the two poles of inaccessibility — precisely the pairing Paul needs. Amos thus supplies the alternative illustration that replaces Moses's sea.

Moses: heaven (unattainable) — sea (unavailable).Amos 9:2: heaven — Sheol.Paul: heaven (unattainable, citing Moses) — Sheol (unavailable, citing Amos).The Mosaic principle is preserved exactly. Only the illustrative term for unavailability changes, from the sea to Sheol.

D. The Three Parts of Christ's Humanity at Death

The reason Paul must use Sheol rather than the sea is anatomical and historical: after the physical death of the Lord Jesus Christ, the three components of His humanity went in three separate directions.

First, the body of Christ went into the grave (Luke 23:53). Second, the spirit of Christ went into the presence of God the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46). Third, the soul of Christ went into Sheol — specifically into the compartment called paradise or Abraham's bosom (Psalm 16:10; Luke 23:43; Acts 2:27; Ephesians 4:9).

Sheol as a whole has three compartments. Paradise (Abraham's bosom) held the Old Testament believers. Across a great gulf lay Hades, the location of unbelieving dead. A third compartment, Tartarus, held certain angelic creatures who followed Satan in the original rebellion (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). In the resurrection, the soul of Christ came up from paradise in Sheol to rejoin the body in the grave, while His spirit returned from the Father. Body, soul, and spirit were reunited in resurrection — a literal, bodily, physical resurrection.

Because resurrection involved the soul of Christ ascending from Sheol — not from the sea — Paul cannot use Moses's sea illustration in connection with the first advent. The resurrection came up out of Sheol. The sea is irrelevant to the historical event Paul is now referencing. Therefore Paul goes to Amos 9:2 for an illustration that accurately reflects what occurred.

E. The First Advent as the Pivotal Historical Factor

In the time of Moses, the first advent was prophetical — eschatological. Jewish inability to perceive its full import was neither a failure nor a culpable blindness; the event had not yet occurred. In the time of Paul, the first advent was historical. Every element of Code X2 of the Mosaic Law — every animal sacrifice, every tabernacle typology, every holy day, every priestly function — had been fulfilled by the Lord Jesus Christ. His death on the cross completed the spiritual death that bore the sins of mankind; His physical death followed only after salvation was accomplished, signaled by the words

Tetelestai (Τετέλεσται) — it has been completed in the past with the result that it stands completed forever (John 19:30).

Because the first advent is now historical when Paul writes, Paul is in a position to be stronger than Moses. Moses could speak of salvation as near — and that was already as strong a statement as could be made on the basis of prophecy. Paul can say the same and add: and the event that makes it so is already accomplished history. The Jews of Paul's day therefore have even less excuse than Israel had between Sinai and the first advent — and they had no excuse then.

V. The Jewish Failure: The Great Blot-Out

The first advent of the Lord Jesus Christ is the central event of human history. Yet the unbelieving Jews of Paul's day had systematically expunged it from their frame of reference — the great blot-out. This expulsion took two forms.

First, they had distorted the Mosaic Law. Code X2, which functioned exclusively as a typological and prophetic system pointing to faith in the coming Messiah, was reinterpreted as a system of meritorious works for divine acceptance. The animal sacrifices were treated as rituals generating standing before God rather than as portrayals of the substitutionary atonement. The keeping of the commandments was treated as the basis of righteousness rather than as the standard that condemned and drove the conscientious Israelite to faith.

Second, they had blotted out the first advent itself. Every seeking Jew who attempted to be saved by keeping the law was, in effect, asserting that the Messiah had not yet come — that the first advent had not occurred or had not accomplished what it in fact accomplished. To re-enact the animal sacrifices after the cross is to say that the cross was insufficient. To seek salvation by the law after Calvary is to demand that Christ descend from heaven again or rise from the dead again — as though His work had not been done.

Paul's citation of Deuteronomy 30 in Romans 10:6–8 is therefore not merely an exegetical tour de force; it is a direct charge against Jewish unbelief. The Mosaic Law itself — the very document the Jews appealed to for their works-righteousness program — condemns that program and points to faith in Christ as the only acceptable response.

VI. Universal Availability of Salvation

The principle that salvation is as near as mouth and right lobe — body and soul — has an implication that extends far beyond the Jewish situation Paul is addressing. It is a principle of universal scope.

Every human being who has ever lived possesses a body (mouth) and a soul (right lobe). Wherever God consciousness exists — the innate awareness that God is — God takes responsibility to provide sufficient information for a response of faith. Positive volition at God consciousness triggers the provision of additional revelation: the gospel reaches the positive volition wherever it is, however remote the geography. Geographical isolation is no barrier to divine provision. Every person who has ever perished under persecution, famine, war, or historical catastrophe had the same fundamental opportunity as any person in any privileged setting.

Negative volition, by contrast, sets in motion the degeneration described in Romans 1:18–32. Sustained negative volition at God consciousness produces cultural and civilizational regression — idolatry, demonism, the abandonment of truth — which is the historical cause, not the excuse, for spiritual deprivation. The deprived are not deprived because God withheld access; they are deprived because their volition, individually and collectively, rejected what was available.

Conversely, there is no person who arrives in eternal condemnation who did not have every opportunity not to do so. The justice of God — which is the axis of this entire epistle — is perfectly satisfied on both sides: in salvation provided through imputed divine righteousness, and in judgment that falls only on those who, having had opportunity, declined the provision.

VII. Moses and Paul — A Comparative Summary

The following chart summarizes the structural relationship between Deuteronomy 30 and Romans 10:

Category Moses (Deuteronomy 30) Paul (Romans 10)
Unattainable pole Heaven (v.12) Heaven — to bring Christ down (Rom. 10:6)
Unavailable pole Across the sea (v.13) Sheol/Hades — to bring Christ up from the dead (Rom. 10:7)
Basis of change Prophetical first advent Historical first advent; soul of Christ came from Sheol in resurrection
Conclusion Salvation near: mouth and heart (v.14) Salvation near: mouth and right lobe (Rom. 10:8)

Both Moses and Paul arrive at the same destination: salvation is not unattainable and not unavailable. It is as near as the believer's own body and soul. Paul's contribution is to show that since the first advent has occurred historically, the nearness of salvation is even more incontrovertible than it was in Moses's day — and therefore the inexcusability of unbelief is even greater.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Two

1. Salvation through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ is both attainable and available: not in heaven (therefore not unattainable) and not across the sea or in Sheol (therefore not unavailable). Moses establishes this; Paul confirms and amplifies it.

2. The structure of Deuteronomy 30:11–14 is a premise followed by three conclusions: (v.11) the commandment is not too difficult or too far away; (v.12) not in heaven; (v.13) not across the sea; (v.14) it is near — in mouth and heart.

3. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:12 in Romans 10:6 exactly, but adds the historical implication of the first advent: that is, to bring Christ down from heaven. Moses speaks prophetically; Paul speaks from history.

4. Paul changes Moses's sea analogy to Sheol in Romans 10:7, drawing on Amos 9:2, because in the resurrection the soul of Christ ascended from paradise in Sheol — not from the sea. The substitution is historically and anatomically precise.

5. At physical death, the three components of Christ's humanity separated: His body went to the grave (Luke 23:53), His spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46), and His soul to paradise in Sheol (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27). In resurrection, all three were reunited in the glorified body.

6. Sheol comprises three compartments: paradise (Abraham's bosom), where Old Testament believers resided; Hades, the location of unbelieving dead; and Tartarus, where certain fallen angelic creatures are confined. Christ's soul was in paradise, not Hades.

7. In the time of Moses, the first advent was prophetical; in the time of Paul, it was historical. This shift makes Paul's argument stronger than Moses's while maintaining complete continuity with it.

8. Every time an unbelieving Jew seeks salvation by works of the law, he implicitly denies the first advent — asserting, in effect, that Christ has not yet come and that His work was not efficacious. This constitutes the great blot-out and is tantamount to blasphemy against the God of Israel.

9. God accepts only His own righteousness. Self-righteousness and works-righteousness — whether expressed as law-keeping, moral attainment, or civilizational achievement — are never the basis for divine blessing in time or in eternity. The Jews' highest culture and intellectual accomplishment cannot substitute for imputed divine righteousness.

10. Paul's Old Testament documentation establishes: faith in Christ results in the imputation of divine righteousness (δικαιοσύνη θεού, *dikaiosynē theou*). Once that imputation is received, every subsequent attempt to supplement it with self-righteousness is both futile and arrogant.

11. The availability of salvation is universal. Every human being possesses a soul (right lobe, the capacity for faith) and a body (mouth, the capacity for expression). Wherever positive volition toward God exists, God provides sufficient revelation for a response of faith. Geographical isolation, historical tragedy, and cultural privation are no barrier to divine provision.

12. There is no person in eternal condemnation who lacked the opportunity for salvation. The justice of God is perfectly satisfied: provision was made through imputed divine righteousness for all who believe; judgment falls only on those who, having had opportunity, exercised negative volition.

13. Negative volition at God consciousness produces cultural regression, as described in Romans 1:18–32. Civilizational privation is the historical consequence of sustained negative volition — not evidence of divine withholding.

14. Romans 10:8 sets up the correct reading of Romans 10:9–10: the mouth and heart of those verses refer to the body and soul as described in Deuteronomy 30:14, not to a public confession formula or a separate requirement for salvation beyond faith.

15. Moses and Paul say the same thing: salvation is not in heaven (unattainable) and not across the sea or in Sheol (unavailable). It is as near as body and soul. The first advent, now historical, makes the case even stronger and the inexcusability of unbelief even greater.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
dabar דָּבָר dabar — word, matter, thing Hebrew noun used in Deuteronomy 30:14 to denote the content of salvation — the gospel doctrine. In Code X2 of the Mosaic Law, dabar refers to the salvific word that is near to every person in mouth and heart.
ʿavar עָבַר ʿavar — to pass over, to cross Qal stem verb used in Deuteronomy 30:13 for crossing the sea. In Paul's adaptation, the analogous concept becomes descending into Sheol — reflecting the historical reality of Christ's resurrection from the underworld rather than emergence from the sea.
laqach לָקַח laqach — to take, to seize and bring Qal perfect used in Deuteronomy 30:13: that he might bring it — salvation — to us. The verb implies purposeful retrieval; Moses pictures someone crossing the sea to obtain and deliver the message of salvation.
shamaʼ שָמַע shamaʼ — to hear, to listen, to obey In Deuteronomy 30:13, used in the Hiphil (causative) stem: to cause to hear, i.e., to communicate authoritatively. Moses causing Israel to hear the law at Sinai is the model; the gospel being caused to reach positive volition is the New Testament application.
ʿasah עָשָה ʿasah — to do, to act, to perform Qal imperfect used in Deuteronomy 30:13–14: that we might do it. In the context of Code X2, doing the commandment means believing in Christ — the non-meritorious act of faith as the required response to the gospel.
Sheol שְאוֹל sheʼol — the underworld The Hebrew term for the abode of the dead, equivalent to the Greek Hades. Sheol has three compartments: paradise (Abraham's bosom), where Old Testament believers resided until the resurrection of Christ; Hades proper, where unbelieving dead await final judgment; and Tartarus, where certain fallen angelic creatures are confined. Paul draws on Amos 9:2 to substitute Sheol for Moses's sea analogy, since the soul of Christ came from paradise in Sheol at the resurrection.
Hades Ἅδης Hades — the underworld, realm of the dead Greek equivalent of Hebrew Sheol. Used by Paul in Romans 10:7 (Αβυσσον, the abyss) to designate the realm from which Christ's soul ascended at the resurrection. Translated "hell" in the King James Version and in the Apostles' Creed, producing considerable confusion; the term properly refers to the intermediate state of the dead, not to the lake of fire.
Tetelestai Τετέλεσται Tetelestai — it has been completed Perfect passive indicative of the Greek verb teleō: it has been completed in the past with the result that it stands completed forever. The word of Christ from the cross (John 19:30) signaling that the work of salvation was fully accomplished before His physical death. Christ died physically only after this declaration.
dikaiosynē theou δικαιοσύνη θεού dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God The divine righteousness imputed to the believer at the moment of salvation adjustment — faith in Christ. God can bless only His own righteousness; therefore imputed divine righteousness is the indispensable basis for all divine blessing in time and in eternity. The central axis of the Epistle to the Romans.
Code X2 (Mosaic Law) The salvation provisions of the Mosaic Law — the second of three divisions: (1) the commandments (moral code), (2) the ordinances (typological and ceremonial provisions pointing to faith in Christ), and (3) the judgments (civil code). Code X2 consists entirely of prophetic and typological material fulfilled by the Lord Jesus Christ in the first advent. It has never been a system of works-righteousness.
God consciousness The innate, universal awareness that God exists, arising from general revelation (creation, conscience). Positive volition at God consciousness triggers God's logistical provision of the gospel. Negative volition at God consciousness initiates the cycle of degeneration described in Romans 1:18–32.
The great blot-out The systematic suppression and denial of the first advent of the Lord Jesus Christ by unbelieving Israel. The blot-out involves both the distortion of the Mosaic Law into a works-righteousness system and the refusal to acknowledge that Code X2 was fulfilled by Christ. It is the root cause of Israel's historical cycles of national discipline.
Adjustment to the justice of God The mechanism by which divine blessing is received. Three categories: (1) salvation adjustment — faith in Christ, instantaneous and once only; (2) rebound adjustment — naming known sins to God, restoring fellowship (1 John 1:9); (3) maturity adjustment — progressive intake of Bible doctrine resulting in spiritual growth toward supergrace.

Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Three

Romans 10:6 — Faith Righteousness versus Self-Righteousness; Moses and Paul on the Attainability of Salvation

Romans 10:6 “But the righteousness based on faith says, 'Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?"' (that is, to bring Christ down)” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But the righteousness which is by means of faith communicates in this manner: Do not think in your right lobe, Who shall ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down from above.

Romans 10:6 stands at the pivot between Paul's summary indictment of Jewish works-righteousness (vv. 1–5) and the celebrated salvation passage of verses 9–10. In this chapter we complete the exegetical groundwork laid in preceding sessions — the relationship between Deuteronomy 30:11–14 and Romans 10:6–8 — and advance into the detailed analysis of verse 6b. The central interpretive issue is why Paul substitutes the Sheol analogy of Amos 9:2 for the sea analogy of Moses, and what that substitution reveals about the first advent of Christ as the decisive turning point in Jewish religious history.

I. Deuteronomy 30:11–14 and Romans 10:6–8: The Parallel Structure

The exegetical complexity of Romans 10:6–8 arises from Paul's dual operation on the Mosaic text: he quotes it, amplifies it in light of the first advent, and in one instance replaces Moses's illustration with one drawn from Amos. Understanding the parallel structure is prerequisite to interpreting any individual phrase.

The Correspondence of Verses

Moses in Deuteronomy 30:12 is quoted by Paul in Romans 10:6. Moses in Deuteronomy 30:13 is replaced by Paul in Romans 10:7, with the sea analogy exchanged for Sheol. Moses in Deuteronomy 30:14 is quoted and interpreted by Paul in Romans 10:8. In verse 12 Paul makes a nearly exact quotation and then adds an implication grounded in the first advent. In verse 13 he deliberately alters the illustration. In verse 14 he supplies the true interpretation of Moses's intent.

Corrected Translation of Deuteronomy 30:11–14

Verse 11: For this commandment — the commandment to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ — which I command you today is not too difficult for you, not unattainable, not too far away, not unavailable.

Verse 12: It is not in heaven, so that you must say, Who will go up to heaven for us, that he may bring salvation to us and cause us to hear it, so that we might do it — that is, believe in Christ.

Verse 13: Neither is salvation over the sea, so that you must say, Who will cross the sea for us, that he may bring salvation to us and cause us to hear it, so that we might do it — that is, believe in Christ.

Verse 14: But the word — salvation through faith in Christ — is very near you: in your mouth, that is, the body; and in your heart, that is, the right lobe; that you may do it — that is, believe in Christ.

II. Why Paul Replaces the Sea with Sheol

The substitution of Sheol for the sea is not arbitrary. Paul writes under the ministry of the Holy Spirit and remains within the boundaries of Old Testament analogy. The authorization for the change comes from Amos 9:2, which reads: Though they dig into Sheol, from there shall my hand take them; and though they ascend to heaven, from there I will bring them down. Amos already pairs heaven and Sheol as the two extremes of inaccessibility, the same pairing implicit in Moses's heaven and sea. Paul therefore replaces Moses's sea with Amos's Sheol without abandoning the Mosaic principle; he amplifies it.

The Theological Reason for the Change

In the time of Moses, the first advent of Christ was prophetic. Accordingly, Moses's sea analogy carried the full weight of the unavailability illustration without any reference to where Christ's soul would travel. In the time of Paul, the first advent was history. After the death of the Lord Jesus Christ, the three components of His humanity went in three directions: His body went into the tomb (Luke 23:53); His spirit went into the presence of God the Father in heaven (Luke 23:46); His soul descended to Sheol — specifically to the compartment called paradise or Abraham's bosom (Psalm 16:10; Luke 23:43; Acts 2:27; Ephesians 4:9). In the resurrection, the soul and spirit of the Lord Jesus Christ rejoined the glorified body, and the soul ascended from Sheol. Paul cannot use the sea analogy in connection with the resurrection because Christ was not resurrected from the sea; He came up from Sheol. Amos 9:2 supplies precisely the term Paul requires.

The Three Compartments of Sheol/Hades

Sheol in Hebrew — transliterated

Sheol in Hebrew (שְׁאוֹל, transliterated she'ol) corresponds to Hades (ᾅδης) in Greek. The term designates the underworld in its totality, which Scripture presents as consisting of three compartments. The first, called paradise or Abraham's bosom, was the temporary residence of Old Testament believers and the destination of Christ's soul at death. A great gulf fixed separates it from the second compartment, called the place of torments, which houses the souls of unbelievers from all ages. The third compartment is Tartarus (Τάρταρος, Tartaros), reserved for certain categories of fallen angels (2 Peter 2:4). After the resurrection and ascension of Christ, the believers held in paradise were transferred to the third heaven (Ephesians 4:8–10), so that the paradise compartment of Sheol is no longer occupied.

Summary of the Analogical Correspondence

Heaven in Moses = unattainable; heaven in Paul = unattainable, with the additional implication that to seek to bring salvation down from heaven is to deny that Christ has already descended in the incarnation. The sea in Moses = unavailable; Sheol in Paul = unavailable, with the additional implication that to seek to bring salvation up from the depths is to deny that Christ has already risen in the resurrection. The principle Moses taught is preserved intact and amplified by the historical facts of the first advent.

III. The Big Blot Out: Jewish Rejection of the First Advent

The reason Paul must amplify Moses at all is that his contemporaries — and the Jewish community from the apostolic era forward — had systematically erased from their theological consciousness the historical reality of the first advent of the Lord Jesus Christ. This erasure Paul designates functionally as the great distortion: knowing the righteousness of God but refusing to submit to it, substituting instead a works-righteousness derived from keeping the Mosaic law.

The Mosaic law consisted of three codices. Codex one, the Decalogue, set forth the moral standard. Codex two, the ordinances, contained an elaborate typological Christology and soteriology: the Levitical offerings, the Day of Atonement, the Passover, the Levitical priesthood, the table of showbread — every element pointed to the cross, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ. Codex three comprised the social regulations governing Israel as a national entity. The unbelieving Jew across both dispensations elevated Codex one and Codex three into a system of salvation while blotting out the Christological content of Codex two. In Paul's time and continuously thereafter, this same negative volition is directed against the historical fulfillment of Codex two in the person and work of Christ.

The consequence of this sustained negative volition is not merely theological error but historical catastrophe. Every major persecution endured by the Jewish people — from the fall of Jerusalem in 70 A.D. through the pogroms of imperial Russia, the expulsions of the medieval period, and the Nazi Holocaust of 1933–1945 — is traceable to the same root cause: the rejection of the righteousness of God made available through faith in the Messiah. This is not an indictment but an explanation, and Paul himself, the Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), makes it with grief rather than contempt (Romans 10:1).

IV. Exegesis of Romans 10:6b

The Prohibition: Think Not

The clause opens with the aorist active subjunctive of legō (λέγω) plus the negative mē (μή). The verb legō means to speak or to say, but in this context functions idiomatically for the formation of words in thought — the activity of the right lobe prior to verbal expression. The corrected translation is therefore think not rather than say not. The aorist tense contemplates the action of the verb in its totality and forbids it by means of the negative mē, producing what grammarians call the subjunctive of prohibition. The active voice assigns the production of the forbidden action to the subject — in this case the Jewish audience addressed. The prohibition is comprehensive: the rationalization that salvation is unattainable is forbidden at its source, in the right lobe, before it can be verbalized.

In Your Right Lobe

The prepositional phrase en tē kardia sou (ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου) employs en plus the locative of kardia (καρδία). The term kardia never denotes the physiological organ in the New Testament. It consistently designates the right lobe of the soul — the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, and the norms and standards constituting the conscience. The possessive genitive singular of the personal pronoun sou (σου) — your — emphasizes that the activity of believing, like the activity of rationalizing, is irreducibly personal. No one can believe on behalf of another. The right lobe is both the source of faith and the source of rationalization; the two occupy the same cognitive space, and the choice between them is an act of volition.

Who Shall Ascend into Heaven?

The quotation continues with the interrogative pronoun tis (τίς) followed by the future middle indicative of anabainō (ἀναβαίνω), with the prepositional phrase eis ton ouranon (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν): Who shall ascend into heaven? The future tense here is deliberative rather than strictly temporal — it expresses uncertainty about the agent of an action rather than simple futurity. The middle voice emphasizes the subject as producer of the action. The phrase is drawn almost verbatim from Deuteronomy 30:12, where Moses asked rhetorically whether salvation was inaccessibly remote. Paul retains the rhetorical force but adds the interpretive gloss: that is, to bring Christ down from above. The rationalization that someone must ascend to bring salvation down is now exposed as a denial of the incarnation. Christ has already descended from heaven. The first advent is history. To demand that salvation come down from heaven is to treat the incarnation as though it had not occurred — it is the theological expression of the big blot out.

V. The Theological Stakes: Faith Righteousness versus Self-Righteousness

The entire passage from Romans 10:1 through 10:8 turns on the antithesis between two kinds of righteousness. Paul states this antithesis in verse 3: not knowing the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. The right lobe is the battlefield. Faith and rationalization occupy the same cognitive space, and the outcome of their conflict determines whether a person receives imputed righteousness through faith in Christ or pursues a self-manufactured righteousness that God can never accept.

Arrogance is the root of every form of works-righteousness. The person who says, I will be saved by keeping the law, or by moral behavior, or by religious ceremony, is saying in effect that his own resources are sufficient to satisfy the justice of God. That is the definition of arrogance in its most dangerous form — arrogance directed against the plan of God. Arrogance and grace are mutually exclusive. Grace says that God's provision in Christ is sufficient; arrogance says that human effort can supplement or replace it.

The rationalization of unattainability — who shall ascend into heaven? — is simply arrogance translated into religious vocabulary. It implies that the standard is too high, that the gap between the human and the divine is unbridgeable, and that therefore the only practical option is to do what one can with the resources at hand. But Moses anticipated this rationalization and refuted it: salvation is not in heaven, it is as near as your right lobe and your mouth. Paul confirms it: the same salvation is even nearer now, because the first advent is historical rather than prophetic.

The universality of this principle must be stressed. Salvation is not a geographical, cultural, or linguistic privilege. It is a right-lobe issue. Whether the person in question inhabits the intellectual world of fifth-century Athens, the ritual world of first-century Jerusalem, or the most isolated human community on earth, salvation is as near as his capacity to think and to choose. The corollary from Romans 1 — that every human being has been given sufficient cognitive endowment to respond to the revelation God has provided — means that no human being ever faces the justice of God without having had a genuine opportunity to believe. The one exception is the person who lacks the cognitive capacity to form belief at all; such a person is not held responsible for a decision he is constitutionally incapable of making.

VI. Christ as the Termination of the Law (Romans 10:4)

The rationalization exposed in verse 6 — who shall ascend into heaven to bring Christ down? — contradicts the explicit statement of verse 4. The corrected translation of Romans 10:4 reads: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness, to each one because he believes. The Greek word translated termination is

The Greek word translated termination is telos (τέλος), which carries the sense of completion, fulfillment, and goal. Christ is not merely the chronological end of the law's period of applicability; He is its fulfillment in the sense that everything the law pointed toward — especially Codex two — has been accomplished in His person and work. To attempt salvation through law-keeping after the cross is therefore not merely futile; it is a contradiction of what the law itself was designed to communicate. Every Levitical offering, every function of the Day of Atonement, every Passover observance was a pointer to the Lord Jesus Christ. To treat those pointers as the destination rather than the direction is to have missed the entire pedagogical purpose of Codex two.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Three

1. Paul's amplification of Moses is authorized by the Holy Spirit and grounded in Old Testament analogy. The change from Moses's sea illustration to the Sheol illustration of Amos 9:2 does not alter the Mosaic principle; it amplifies it by incorporating the historical facts of the first advent. Heaven and Sheol in Paul correspond precisely to heaven and sea in Moses: one illustration of the unattainable, one of the unavailable.

2. The substitution of Sheol for the sea is theologically necessary. Because Christ's soul descended to the Sheol compartment called paradise at death and ascended from it in the resurrection, only the Sheol analogy — not the sea analogy — can carry the implication that to demand a repeated descent is to deny the historical resurrection. Paul could not have made this point with Moses's sea illustration.

3. The verb legō in verse 6 is correctly translated think not, not say not. The prohibition targets the formation of the rationalization in the right lobe before it reaches verbal expression. The subjunctive of prohibition with the negative mē forbids the action comprehensively. Words are formed from thought; the source of erroneous theology is erroneous thinking, and the prohibition goes to the source.

4. Kardia consistently designates the right lobe of the soul throughout the New Testament. It never refers to the physiological organ. The right lobe is the seat of the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, conscience, and — critically — both faith and rationalization. The conflict between salvation adjustment and self-righteousness is fought and decided in this faculty.

5. The deliberative future in tis anabēsetai expresses uncertainty about the agent of an action. The question who shall ascend? is not a prediction but a rationalization — the language of negative volition seeking to excuse its rejection of available divine provision by treating that provision as if it were inaccessible.

6. The rationalization of unattainability is the linguistic form of arrogance directed against the plan of God. To say who shall ascend into heaven? is to imply that salvation requires heroic human initiative rather than simple faith. Every form of works-righteousness — whether law-keeping, ritual observance, moral effort, or religious ceremony — rests on this same rationalization. Arrogance and grace are mutually exclusive. Grace declares the provision complete; arrogance insists on contributing to it.

7. Faith and rationalization occupy the same cognitive location: the right lobe. This is why salvation is as near as a person's own mind and why no person has a valid excuse. The decision between faith in the righteousness of God imputed through Christ and the pursuit of self-righteousness is made in the right lobe, within the cognitive reach of every human being possessing the capacity for thought.

8. The universality of available salvation is established by the logic of Moses confirmed by Paul. Salvation is not geographically, culturally, or linguistically limited. It is a right-lobe issue, equally accessible to every person who possesses the cognitive capacity to believe. The one category exempted from responsibility is the person who genuinely lacks the cognitive capacity to form belief. All others stand without excuse before the justice of God.

9. Christ as the termination of the law (Romans 10:4) renders law-keeping as a means of salvation self-contradictory. Codex two of the Mosaic law was an elaborate Christological and soteriological system pointing to the cross, resurrection, and ascension. Every element of that Codex has been fulfilled. To attempt salvation through Codex one or three after the fulfillment of Codex two is to use the pointer as a destination and to treat the fulfillment as though it had not occurred — the precise error Paul is exposing.

10. The historical transition from Moses to Paul transforms the status of the first advent from prophetic to historical. In Moses's time, Jewish blindness to the coming Messiah was a failure to read Codex two correctly. In Paul's time and thereafter, Jewish rejection of Christ compounds that failure by blotting out an event that is now historical fact. The implications of this blot-out are traceable across the subsequent centuries of Jewish history, constituting the deepest explanatory framework for the recurring pattern of national catastrophe.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
legō λέγω legō — to say, to speak; idiomatically, to think or form words in the mind Present active verb meaning to speak or to say. In Romans 10:6 Paul uses it idiomatically for the formation of thought in the right lobe prior to verbal expression, supporting the corrected translation think not rather than say not.
mē μή mē — the negative particle used with the subjunctive mood The negative particle that, combined with the aorist subjunctive, forms the subjunctive of prohibition — a comprehensive forbidding of the action of the verb in its totality. Distinguished from ou, which negates indicative statements of fact.
kardia καρδία kardia — heart; the right lobe of the soul Never used in the New Testament for the physiological heart. Consistently designates the right lobe of the soul: the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, conscience, and the seat of both faith and rationalization.
anabainō ἀναβαίνω anabainō — to ascend, to go up Compound verb: ana (up) + bainō (to go). Used in the deliberative future tense in Romans 10:6, expressing uncertainty about the agent of an action rather than simple futurity. The question tis anabēsetai — who shall ascend? — is a rationalization, not a prediction.
ouranos οὐρανός ouranos — heaven Used in Romans 10:6 as the analogy for the unattainable. Moses employed heaven in Deuteronomy 30:12 to demonstrate that salvation is not inaccessibly remote. Paul retains the analogy and adds the implication that to seek to bring Christ down from heaven is to deny the historical reality of the incarnation.
telos τέλος telos — end, termination, goal, fulfillment Used in Romans 10:4: Christ is the telos of the law with reference to righteousness. Carries the dual sense of chronological termination and purposive fulfillment. Christ fulfills what the law — especially Codex two — pointed toward, rendering law-keeping as a means of salvation both obsolete and self-contradictory.
she'ol / Hades שְׁאוֹל / ᾅδης she'ol (Hebrew) / Hadēs (Greek) — the underworld; the realm of the dead The term designates the underworld in its totality. Scripture presents it as consisting of three compartments: paradise (Abraham's bosom), the temporary residence of Old Testament believers and the destination of Christ's soul at death; the place of torments, housing the souls of unbelievers; and Tartarus, reserved for certain fallen angels. Paul substitutes the Sheol analogy of Amos 9:2 for Moses's sea analogy because Christ's soul ascended from Sheol, not from the sea, in the resurrection.
tis τίς tis — who? which one? (interrogative pronoun) The interrogative pronoun introducing the deliberative question of Romans 10:6b: Who shall ascend into heaven? The deliberative usage expresses uncertainty about the agent rather than the timing of the action, functioning rhetorically as the language of rationalization rather than inquiry.

Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Four

Romans 10:6 — The Parenthetical Implication: Bringing Christ Down from Heaven

Romans 10:6 “But the righteousness based on faith says, 'Do not say in your heart, “Who will ascend into heaven?”' (that is, to bring Christ down)” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But the righteousness which is by means of faith communicates in this manner: 'Do not think in your right lobe, who shall ascend into heaven?' — the implication being, to bring Christ down from heaven.

This chapter continues the verse-by-verse study of Romans 10, having reached the final clause of verse 6, where Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30:12 and appends a parenthetical implication not present in Moses's original text. The previous session completed the first ten principles governing Paul's interpretive method. This chapter resumes with point eleven and concludes the exposition of verse 6, establishing the transition to verse 7.

I. Review of Points 1–10: The Interpretive Framework

The first ten principles governing Paul's use of Deuteronomy 30:12 were established in the preceding study. They are summarized here for continuity.

1. Rationalization rejects imputed righteousness.

The phrase 'Do not think in your right lobe, who shall ascend into heaven?' represents a rationalization that rejects Romans 10:4 — Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness for the one who believes.

2. The unbelieving Jew rejects the first advent.

Just as the unbelieving Jew of the Old Testament rejected the message of Codex 2 of the Mosaic law, which offered imputed righteousness through faith, so the unbelieving Jew of the Church Age rejects the historical fulfillment of Codex 2 at the cross.

3. Both dispensations share the same rejection.

In both dispensations, the unbelieving Jew refuses the imputed righteousness of God through faith in Christ and substitutes self-righteousness through keeping the law.

4. The central issue is faith-righteousness versus self-righteousness.

The conflict is between self-works righteousness and the imputed righteousness of God, also designated faith-righteousness.

5. The conflict resides in the right lobe of the soul.

Negative volition is represented by rationalization; positive volition is represented by faith. These are two competing systems of perception operating within the soul.

6. Paul draws on Moses's warning in Deuteronomy 30:11–14.

7. Moses foresaw the distortion of Codex 2.

Jewish arrogance and negative volition would quickly distort Codex 1 and Codex 3 of the Mosaic law into a system of works-righteousness that God would never accept.

8. The blotting out of the first advent recurs across history.

Just as the negative-volition Jew blotted the true function of Codex 2 from his mind in Moses's time, so the negative-volition Jew would blot out the first advent of Christ in Paul's time and thereafter.

9. Ritual without reality was the mechanism of rejection.

The unbelieving Jew from Moses to Christ blotted out Codex 2 by emphasizing animal sacrifice as ritual while excluding the reality it anticipated — the saving work of Christ on the cross.

10. Salvation is as near as the right lobe.

The soul's right lobe — containing the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary and categorical storage, and norms and standards — is the arena in which faith and rationalization contend. Faith is non-meritorious and uses divine revelation as its object; rationalization uses human reason to ignore, distort, and reject that revelation.

II. Continuation: Points 11–15 on Moses and Paul

11. Moses anticipated rejection of the first advent.

Even in the time of Moses, the unbelieving Jew rejected the first advent of Christ. Isaiah confirmed this pattern centuries later: 'Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?' (Isaiah 53:1). What Moses anticipated at the founding of the client nation Israel was perpetuated through the prophetic period.

12. Unbelieving Jews sought the millennium without salvation.

They wanted the crown without the cross. They desired the fulfillment of the unconditional covenants and the blessings of the messianic kingdom while bypassing the cross entirely. The millennium cannot be obtained apart from the cross, and the crown cannot be obtained apart from salvation.

13. Ritual without reality is the form of this rejection.

Animal sacrifice practiced without faith in what it represented was ritual without reality. To offer animal sacrifices without believing in the atoning death of Christ they prefigured was the precise form of Codex 2 rejection in the Old Testament.

14. The millennium without salvation means blotting out the first advent.

The Jews desired the second advent and the unconditional covenant fulfillments apart from faith in Christ and apart from the cross. This has been their characteristic error across every dispensation.

15. The crown without the cross is the analogical formulation.

In the right lobe of the Jewish unbeliever, blotting out the first advent is equivalent to seeking the crown while bypassing the cross.

III. The Parenthetical Addition: Paul's Amplification of Moses

16. Paul amplifies Moses's warning for the Church Age.

The wild rationalization first identified by Moses in Deuteronomy 30:12 is now amplified by Paul in Romans 10:6. Everything in verse 6 up to this point is drawn from that Mosaic text. Paul now adds something Moses did not include, because Paul writes from the vantage point of historical fulfillment rather than prophetic anticipation.

17. The first advent was prophetic to Moses but historical to Paul.

Moses looked forward to the cross and gave its implications in anticipatory terms. Paul looks back to the cross and gives its implications in historical terms. Both accept the cross; the Jewish unbeliever in every generation blots it out. The King James Version places Paul's addition in parentheses, signaling that it is not part of the Deuteronomy quotation.

IV. Grammatical Analysis of the Parenthetical Clause

The Demonstrative Pronoun and the Verb 'to Be'

The clause opens with touto (τοῦτο), a nominative neuter singular demonstrative pronoun. The near demonstrative — touto (this) rather than the distant ekeino (that) — emphasizes the immediacy of the implication. It is joined with the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί), the verb 'to be.' Taken literally, the phrase reads 'that is' or 'this is.' However, this is an idiomatic construction. The idiom means 'this implies' or 'this means.' The correct rendering is: this implies, not merely 'that is.'

The Aorist Infinitive katagō

Following the idiom comes the aorist active infinitive katagō (καταγαγεῖν), from kataagō — to bring down, to lead down. The constative aorist contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety. The active voice indicates that the rationalizing Jewish unbeliever produces the action. The infinitive functions as a conceived result — a consequence assumed to follow from the nature of the rationalization itself. The accusative singular direct object is Christon (Χριστόν), Christ. Since heaven has already been mentioned in the quotation from Deuteronomy, the full phrase is understood: to bring Christ down from heaven.

The Jew who continues to look for the coming of Messiah, even though Messiah came nearly two thousand years ago, is still looking for what has already become historical. In his soul, he has blotted out the reality of the fulfillment of all the principles contained in Codex 2.

V. Theological Implications of 'Bringing Christ Down from Heaven'

1. To bring Christ down from heaven is to reject the historical first advent.

The phrase means to ignore, reject, and blot out the first advent of Christ with all its implications for eternal salvation. In the conflict of the right lobe, faith in Christ receives the imputed righteousness of God; rationalization substitutes a system of self-righteousness or works. The great issue remains: God's righteousness versus self-righteousness.

2. Faith in salvation has an object, and that object is the Lord Jesus Christ.

Saving faith is exercised in the soul, not by any physical act or posture. Location, circumstance, and physical condition are irrelevant. 'Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and you shall be saved' is accomplished entirely within the soul, by a non-meritorious act of the will directed toward the person and work of Christ.

3. The Jewish rejection of the first advent is persistent across history.

From Paul's day to the present, the problem of the Jewish unbeliever is rejection, ignoring, and blotting out the first advent. This rationalization is structurally identical to that employed by their forebears in the time of Moses.

4. This rationalization is tantamount to rejection of Christ as Savior.

5. The rationalization blots out the first advent both prophetically and historically.

It blots it out as prophecy — Isaiah 53 and Codex 2 — in the Old Testament era, and blots it out as history in the days of Paul and thereafter.

6. Ritual without reality obscured the first advent in Moses's time.

Animal sacrifice, the Levitical priesthood, the Day of Atonement, and the Passover were all ritual teaching the coming reality of the cross. The unbelieving Jew observed the ritual while rejecting the reality it signified — the atoning work of Christ.

7. Christ is both the beginning and the end of the law.

Christ is the beginning of the law as the God of Israel who gave the Mosaic law on Sinai. He is the end of the law as the Savior of Israel who fulfilled Codex 2 at the cross. The same Lord Jesus Christ who was judged on the cross for human sin is the divine Person who gave the law to Moses.

8. The Jewish problem in Paul's time is blotting out the first advent through substitution.

The unbelieving Jew will accept Christ as a religious leader or a historical figure, but refuses to accept Him as Messiah and Savior. In place of the cross, a system of personal righteousness through law-keeping is substituted.

9. Historical disaster has followed from the pattern of rejection.

The consistent principle of divine justice is that the righteousness of God cannot be ignored without consequence. The mechanics of rejection — from the hardening of Pharaoh's heart to subsequent national judgments upon Israel — illustrate this principle throughout the Old Testament and into the present age.

VI. The Parenthetical Clause and Its Final Implications

1. The rationalization implies that self-righteousness has the right to ascend into heaven.

The rationalization includes the concept that works-righteousness or self-righteousness earns access to heaven. This is precisely the attitude expressed by the rich young ruler who told Jesus he had kept the law perfectly and asked what more he must do (Mark 10:17–22). The implicit claim was that law-keeping entitled him to heaven.

2. Only the righteousness of God is admitted to heaven.

Since the beginning of recorded Scripture, every person who has believed in the Lord has received the imputation of divine righteousness. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to his account for righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3). The pattern is fixed: the only righteousness that gains entrance to heaven is God's own righteousness, imputed to the believer at the moment of saving faith.

3. Salvation by law-keeping is a blasphemous conclusion.

For a Jew to claim salvation through law-keeping is implicitly to assert that Christ's work was insufficient, or that He was not even the Messiah — i.e., that He must return to complete or even to begin a saving work.

4. This ignores the Lord's declaration of completed atonement.

Our Lord's final cry from the cross was tetelestai (τετέλεσται), recorded in John 19:30. This is the perfect passive indicative of teleō (τελέω), meaning: it has been finished in the past with the result that it stands finished forever. The atonement was completed while Christ was still physically alive on the cross. All the personal sins of human history were imputed to Christ and judged by the Father while He remained physically alive — His spiritual death constituting the judgment. Physical death followed as a voluntary act, not as the ground of atonement.

5. Christ does not return to earth to provide salvation.

He accomplished the work of salvation once and for all at the cross (Hebrews 9:12, 26; 10:10). His return to earth at the second advent has an entirely different purpose: the regathering of Israel, the termination of the times of the Gentiles, and the establishment of the millennial kingdom. These purposes are distinct from and subsequent to the completed atonement.

6. The Church Age is the times of the Gentiles.

The times of the Gentiles extend through the Church Age and through the Tribulation. During this period, only a Gentile nation can serve as a client nation to God. Individual Jews may be saved and may function as evangelists — as the 144,000 Jewish evangelists will during the Tribulation — but no Jewish nation constitutes a client nation to God until Christ returns and His feet stand on the Mount of Olives.

7. Jesus Christ controls history.

The continuation of national blessing, and the forestalling of historical judgment, depends upon two interlocking factors: the pivot of mature believers whose adjustment to the justice of God provides the spiritual infrastructure of the client nation, and the broader population of positive believers whose consistent orientation to doctrine sustains that pivot. Both factors operate under the sovereign control of Jesus Christ over history. The precise threshold at which divine blessing gives way to cycles of national discipline is known only to God.

8. Salvation by works implies the inadequacy of the blood atonement.

Conversely, salvation by faith in Christ affirms the full efficacy of the blood atonement (Ephesians 2:8–9). The two systems are mutually exclusive: any addition of human merit to the basis of salvation is a denial that Christ's work was sufficient.

9. This verse emphasizes that salvation is attainable, not unattainable.

The entire thrust of Paul's argument, drawn from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, is that salvation is near — it is not in a remote or inaccessible location. The soul is the arena, and faith is the means.

10. Blotting out the first advent eliminates salvation entirely.

If the incarnation, the hypostatic union, the cross — redemption, reconciliation, propitiation — are all blotted out from the mind, there is no salvation. The mechanism of blotting out is the instrument of eternal condemnation, self-inflicted through negative volition.

11. The pattern of rejection follows a fixed sequence.

The Jew in the time of Moses, in the time of Paul, and in the present age circumvents the first advent through works-righteousness derived from law-keeping. The sequence is invariable: arrogance produces rationalization, and rationalization produces self-righteousness. This is also the pattern by which liberalism in theology is born — arrogance generates rationalization, which erects a system of human moral achievement in place of the imputed righteousness of God.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Sixty-Four

1. The parenthetical clause in Romans 10:6 is Paul's own addition. Moses in Deuteronomy 30:12 gave the warning against the rationalization. Paul, writing from the vantage point of historical fulfillment, adds the implication: the rationalization amounts to denying the first advent — to demanding that Christ descend from heaven as if He had not already come.

2. The idiomatic phrase 'this implies' governs the parenthetical clause. The demonstrative pronoun touto with eimi functions as an idiom meaning 'this implies' or 'this means,' not merely a literal identification. Paul uses it to draw out the logical consequence of the rationalization described in the Deuteronomy quotation.
