Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
epikaleō ἐπικαλέω epikaleō — to call upon, to invoke Compound verb: epi (upon) + kaleō (to call). Used as a synonym for saving faith in Romans 10:13 and Joel 2:32. The aorist middle subjunctive form epikalesetai indicates a single, contingent act of personal volition directed toward the Lord. Non-meritorious; the merit resides in the object of faith, not the act itself.
sōzō σύζω sōzō — to save, to deliver The standard New Testament verb for salvation and deliverance. In Romans 10:13 the future passive indicative sōthēsetai ('will be saved') converts the conditional protasis into a dogmatic certainty: anyone who calls will certainly be saved. The passive voice indicates that salvation is received, not produced.
pas πᾶς pas — all, every, anyone, whoever Nominative masculine singular adjective used substantivally. In Romans 10:13 it functions as the antecedent of the relative pronoun hos and establishes the universal scope of the gospel offer. No individual or category of person is excluded from either condemnation or the opportunity of salvation.
onoma ὄνομα onoma — name Accusative singular noun. In Romans 10:13, used in the abstract sense of a person about whom one knows the minimum necessary for faith. Indicates that exhaustive theological knowledge is not a prerequisite for salvation. Used as a direct synonym for the person of Jesus Christ in Acts 5:41 and 3 John 7.
gar γάρ gar — for, because (explanatory) Post-positive conjunctive particle. When used in the explanatory sense, as in Romans 10:13, it introduces a reason, ground, or documentary support for a preceding statement. Here it connects the Old Testament citation from Joel 2:32 to Paul's assertion that Christ is Lord of all.
big blot out Technical term for the sustained negative volition of Israel toward the Lord Jesus Christ, specifically the pattern of accepting His Alpha Glory (miraculous works, divine power) while rejecting His Omega Glory (substitutionary death on the cross, resurrection, and saving work). Produces scar tissue of the soul and, at the national level, results in the administration of the five cycles of divine discipline.
Alpha Glory / Omega Glory Alpha Glory refers to the visible works and power of Christ — miracles, signs, the exercise of divine authority. Omega Glory refers to the redemptive work of Christ on the cross, His resurrection, and His present session at the right hand of the Father. The big blot out consists in accepting the former while rejecting the latter.
scar tissue of the soul Accumulated hardness in the right lobe of the soul produced by sustained negative volition toward Bible doctrine and toward the person of Christ. Progresses through the stages of blackout of the soul and ultimately produces the vacuum of the soul. At the national level, a large pivot of souls with scar tissue removes the spiritual protection that moderates historical judgment.
rebound Technical term for the recovery of fellowship with God and the filling of the Holy Spirit through the acknowledgment of known sins to God (1 John 1:9). Instantaneous and repeatable. Requires no emotional response, no promise of future improvement, and no penance. Based on the judicial principle that sins judged at the cross cannot be imputed again (law of double jeopardy). The second of the seven judgments of history.
five cycles of discipline Progressive stages of national divine discipline administered by God against a client nation whose pivot of negative volition has reached a critical threshold. The fifth cycle, the most severe, involves complete historical destruction: military defeat, removal from the land, and national dissolution. Administered against Israel through Assyria (721 BC), Babylon (586 BC), and Rome (AD 70).
pivot The body of mature believers in a national entity whose adjustment to the justice of God sustains divine blessing on the nation and moderates historical judgment. The size and spiritual maturity of the pivot determines the degree to which a nation is protected from the cycles of discipline.
baptism of fire The judgment of living unbelievers at the second advent of Christ, removing them from the earth prior to the establishment of the millennial civilization. Applied separately to Jewish unbelievers (Ezekiel 20:30–38) and Gentile unbelievers (Matthew 25:31–46; Joel 3:1–2). Ensures that the millennium begins with a believing population only.

Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Four

Romans 10:14–15 — Client Nation Responsibility: Evangelism, Missions, and the Pivot

Romans 10:13–14 “For 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (ESV)
Corrected translation: For whoever will call upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How then shall they call upon Him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a herald?

Romans 10 stands as one of the great missionary passages in the New Testament. Having established in verses 9–13 that the same Lord is generous to all who call upon Him — with no distinction between Jew and Gentile — Paul now presses the logical and historical consequences: if calling requires believing, and believing requires hearing, and hearing requires a herald, then the question of who sponsors and sends that herald becomes urgent. Verses 14 and 15 open four interlocking questions that can only be answered within the framework of client nation responsibility. Before entering the verse-by-verse exposition of those questions, two foundational doctrines must be established: the doctrine of the client nation and the principle of the pivot.

I. Review of Romans 10:8–13

Verse 8 quotes Deuteronomy 30:14 to contrast faith-righteousness with works-righteousness: the message of salvation through faith in Christ is near — in the mouth and in the right lobe. Paul identifies this as the message of faith that the apostolic proclamation embodies.

Verse 9 presents a third-class condition: if a person concedes with the mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believes in the right lobe that God raised Him from the dead, that person will be saved. The confession is directed to God, not to a congregation. Verse 10 reinforces the two-sided mechanism: the right lobe believes unto imputed righteousness; the mouth makes the statement to God unto salvation.

Verse 11 quotes Isaiah 28:16: everyone who believes on Him will not be disappointed. Verse 12 removes every racial boundary: there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for the same Lord is generous to all who call upon Him. Verse 13 quotes Joel 2:32 — whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved — confirming that the passage throughout describes Old Testament salvation mechanics applied universally in the Church Age.

II. The Doctrine of the Client Nation

A. Origin and Designation

The term 'client nation' designates a national entity that God has sovereignly assigned a specialized role in His plan for history. In the Old Testament the client nation status of Israel was expressed through the title 'priest-nation.' The referent is not the Levitical priesthood — which was limited to the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron — but the entire national entity functioning in a priestly capacity before the rest of the world.

Exodus 19:5–6 supplies the foundational text: 'Now therefore, if you will obey my doctrine and keep my covenant, then you will be my special possession among all the peoples of the earth, for all the earth is mine. And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.' This declaration was made at Sinai in 1440 BC, when Israel was constituted as the first client nation in history. The phrase 'holy nation' carries the force of 'a nation of integrity' — a national entity set apart to serve God's purposes in the historical arena.

B. The Four Functions of a Client Nation

Four responsibilities define any genuine client nation to God. These functions are interdependent; the removal of any one of them cripples the others.

First, evangelism. The gospel must be communicated within the nation itself. This occurs through several distinct channels: the spiritual gift of evangelism, which enables a believer to hold the attention of unbelievers and present the gospel clearly in a neutral setting; pastoral evangelism, in which pastors communicate the gospel as part of doctrinal teaching to any unbelievers present; and priest-evangelism, the personal witness of every believer functioning in the royal priesthood of the Church Age.

Second, missions. What evangelism accomplishes domestically, missionary activity extends internationally. The client nation provides the logistical base, the financial support, and the personnel for cross-cultural gospel proclamation. Whenever a nation has deteriorated to the point that it can no longer respond to the gospel from within, God's provision is to introduce it from outside through missionaries sent from a functioning client nation.

Third, spiritual growth through the local church or its equivalent. Neither evangelism nor missions produces lasting results without systematic Bible doctrine communicated by a qualified pastor-teacher. Converts must be grounded in doctrine. The local church — or whatever indigenous structure fulfills the same function — is the mechanism through which believers advance to maturity and form the pivot that sustains divine blessing on the nation.

Fourth, the laws of divine establishment. None of the preceding functions can operate without a stable social and political order. Freedom of religion, rule of law, respect for legitimate authority, and the protection of individual volition are prerequisites for the gospel to be heard and for the local church to function. Hosea 4:6 issued the definitive warning: 'My nation is destroyed because of lack of knowledge of doctrine. Because you have rejected the principle of knowing doctrine, I will reject you from being a priest to me.' The Northern Kingdom ignored this warning and Sargon II took Samaria in 721 BC, ending its client nation status. Nebuchadnezzar terminated the Southern Kingdom in 586 BC. The destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD ended any Jewish client nation status for the duration of the present age.

C. The Times of the Gentiles and the Succession of Client Nations

The period extending from the Babylonian captivity to the Second Advent of Christ is designated in Scripture as the Times of the Gentiles. During this period no Jewish national entity can function as a client nation to God. The modern State of Israel exists within the Times of the Gentiles and therefore does not qualify as a client nation, though God's covenantal promises to the Jewish people remain in force and will be fulfilled at the Millennium.

The failure of Israel as client nation did not terminate client nation responsibility in history. It transferred that responsibility to a succession of Gentile nations. During the Babylonian captivity, both Chaldea and the Persian Empire served in a client nation capacity. Subsequently the following national entities fulfilled this role in various degrees: the Roman Empire until its fall in 476 AD; the Frankish kingdom of the Merovingians, reaching its apex under Charlemagne; Ireland and Scotland in the fifth and sixth centuries under the ministries of Patrick and Columba; Sweden during the Thirty Years' War under Gustavus Adolphus; Brandenburg-Prussia under the early Hohenzollerns; Switzerland during the Reformation under Zwingli and Calvin; France during the era of the Huguenots; England during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; and the United States throughout its history.

The pattern is consistent: each of these nations experienced a period of doctrinal vitality, missionary outreach, and historical blessing corresponding to the growth of a functioning pivot of mature believers. Each also experienced decline in proportion to the shrinkage of that pivot and the advance of reversionism among its population.

D. The Future Restoration of Israel as Client Nation

Isaiah 49:5–8 and Isaiah 61:6 anticipate the restoration of Israel as a client nation during the Millennial reign of Christ. Isaiah 61:6 addresses the restored nation directly: 'You will be called priests of Jehovah; you will be spoken of as ministers of our God.' The double portion, the recovery of national honor, and everlasting happiness are promised on the basis of Jehovah's love of justice. Until that restoration, the present age requires Gentile client nations to carry the missionary mandate.

III. The Missionary Function of the Client Nation

A. The Theological Basis

Missionary activity is not an optional program appended to the client nation's responsibilities. It is structurally necessary for two reasons embedded in history. First, internationalism — the consolidation of nations into a single political unit — is a satanic strategy first demonstrated at the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11), which God destroyed directly. The existence of distinct national entities is part of the divine design for history and for the containment of evil. Second, national entities tend toward degeneration with significant speed. When a nation has deteriorated sufficiently that it cannot revitalize itself from within, the only mechanism available under the Protocol Plan of God is external re-evangelization. Missionaries are the instruments of that external re-evangelization.

Jesus Christ controls history in His omniscience. At every point in time He knows where positive volition exists — where people at the point of God consciousness are genuinely open to gospel information in their own language and frame of reference. The client nation that responds to that knowledge by sending qualified personnel fulfills its covenantal obligation. The nation that fails to do so forfeits the historical blessing that attaches to that function.

B. The Historical Record

The missionary history of client nations demonstrates the theological principle concretely. The ministry of Jonah to Nineveh is the most fully documented instance of Old Testament missionary activity. The Assyrians were among the most feared military powers of the ancient Near East, renowned for the severity of their treatment of conquered populations. Their capital Nineveh was not a natural destination for a Jewish prophet. Yet God commissioned Jonah precisely to that location, with a message of coming judgment unless the nation repented.

Jonah's response was initial flight — the direction of Tarshish in Spain being the geographic opposite of Nineveh. The account of the great fish serves the narrative as the mechanism of redirection. Once Jonah delivered the message, the response was city-wide repentance on a scale unparalleled in the prophetic record. The consequences were historical as well as spiritual: the Assyrian empire, instead of collapsing under the fifth cycle of discipline, recovered sufficient internal strength to produce the revival under Tiglath-Pileser III, followed by the reigns of Sargon II and Sennacherib. An empire that would otherwise have been destroyed was preserved for another century through the ministry of a single missionary.

The Frankish kingdom provides a comparable illustration from the post-Roman period. Clovis — whose name appears in the Frankish linguistic tradition as 'Louis' — represented the first generation of Frankish Christian rule. Charlemagne was a third-generation result of that missionary-initiated conversion. Without the prior missionary thrust, neither the Carolingian dynasty nor the political structure of medieval Europe would have taken the form it did.

The missionary expansion of the nineteenth century produced comparable results across multiple continents. The opening of sub-Saharan Africa to the gospel through such figures as Robert Moffat, David Livingstone, and Mary Slessor transformed entire regions that had previously operated under the slave trade and the absence of any ordered civil authority. In each case the missionary fulfilled not only an evangelistic function but also a stabilizing social function, establishing protections for populations that had been exploited systematically.

C. The Quality Requirement for Missionaries

The missionary enterprise requires the highest quality of personnel, not the lowest. The instinct to send those who cannot find a place in domestic ministry to foreign fields has produced systematic damage to the missionary endeavor. The effective missionary must combine mature doctrinal grounding, genuine flexibility in the face of cultural difference, the diplomatic wisdom of a statesman, and the ability to communicate the gospel and doctrine in the language and frame of reference of the target population.

The error of imposing cultural requirements on new converts — demanding that they adopt Western dress, Western family structures, or Western ecclesiastical forms as conditions of Christian identity — has consistently undermined the indigenous development of local churches. The role of doctrine is to transform behavior from within, over time, as believers advance in the spiritual life. The missionary's task is to plant the Word accurately and allow the Holy Spirit and the local culture of believers to produce the appropriate forms of obedience.

The indigenous missionary principle — deploying believers whose linguistic and cultural background aligns with the target population — represents a significant strategic advantage. Church Age believers drawn from diverse ethnic and national backgrounds constitute a resource ideally suited to cross-cultural missionary deployment. The Church Age community is uniquely positioned, in its demographic diversity, to reach populations across the full range of human cultures.

IV. The Pivot and National Preservation

The survival of a client nation is directly proportional to the size and spiritual maturity of its pivot — the body of mature believers whose adjustment to the justice of God through sustained doctrine intake sustains divine blessing on the nation as a whole. A large pivot with a small spin-off of reversionistic believers produces national preservation even under military threat, as demonstrated during the Assyrian invasion of Judah under Sennacherib when the pivot enlarged through the ministry of Isaiah.

Conversely, a small pivot with a large population in reversionism accelerates the progression through the five cycles of discipline toward national destruction. The Northern Kingdom reached the fifth cycle in 721 BC. The Southern Kingdom reached it in 586 BC. The client nation's greatest internal threat is therefore not military or economic but spiritual: the progressive abandonment of Bible doctrine by its believing population.

Positive volition in any generation — the genuine desire to know God and receive His Word — creates the conditions under which God can preserve a nation, delay judgment, and open historical opportunities for missionary advance. Jesus Christ controls history precisely in this sense: His omniscience identifies where positive volition exists at any point on the earth, and His sovereign administration of history allocates resources accordingly. Nations and regions with concentrated positive volition attract missionary activity. Nations with sustained negative volition at the national level exhaust the patience of divine justice and eventually encounter the fifth cycle.

V. Romans 10:14–15 in Context

With these two doctrines established — the client nation and the pivot — the four questions of Romans 10:14–15 can be understood in their full weight. Paul is not posing abstract rhetorical puzzles. He is exposing the chain of responsibility that links the individual who calls upon the name of the Lord all the way back to the decision of a client nation to fund, train, and send qualified gospel messengers.

The first question — 'How then shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed?' — addresses the problem of no gospel hearing: what happens to those who have had no opportunity to hear? The answer involves the full client nation framework. The detailed exegesis of this question and those that follow will be taken up in the next session.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Four

1. Romans 10:13 quotes Joel 2:32 as still in view. The salvation described in Romans 10:9–10 and verse 13 operates on Old Testament mechanics — calling upon the name of the Lord — applied now universally across the Jew-Gentile boundary established in verse 12.

2. The client nation designation is priest-nation. When Israel was constituted at Sinai in 1440 BC, the entire national entity — not merely the Levitical priesthood — was designated a kingdom of priests and a nation of integrity (Exodus 19:5–6). This designation carries four operational responsibilities: evangelism, missions, doctrinal teaching through the local church, and the maintenance of divine establishment.

3. The Times of the Gentiles transfers client nation responsibility. No Jewish national entity can function as a client nation during the Times of the Gentiles. The modern State of Israel exists within this period. Client nation responsibility has passed to a succession of Gentile nations, of which the United States is the present exemplar.

4. Missionary activity is structurally necessary, not optional. Internationalism is satanic in design and national degeneration is rapid. These two factors make external re-evangelization through missionaries a permanent structural requirement of the Protocol Plan of God for the duration of human history. The client nation that sponsors this activity fulfills its covenant obligation; the nation that abandons it accelerates its own decline.

5. The Jonah mission demonstrates the historical consequence of missionary obedience. The ministry of Jonah to Nineveh preserved the Assyrian empire from the fifth cycle of discipline and produced a national revival that extended the empire's viable history by a century. The historical figures of Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, and Sennacherib are the indirect products of a single missionary deployment.

6. Missionary effectiveness requires maturity, not mere willingness. The effective missionary combines advanced spiritual maturity, cultural flexibility, linguistic competence, and the statesmanship that comes from doctrinal application over time. Imposing cultural forms on new converts — rather than allowing doctrine to transform behavior from within — has historically damaged indigenous church development.

7. The pivot of mature believers is the decisive factor in national preservation. The size and spiritual quality of the pivot — those believers who have made the maturity adjustment through sustained doctrine intake — determines whether a client nation receives blessing or discipline. A large pivot postpones or prevents national judgment. A shrinking pivot under reversionism accelerates the progression through the five cycles of discipline.

8. Jesus Christ controls history through His administration of positive volition. In His omniscience Christ knows at every moment where positive volition exists across the earth. His sovereign direction of history channels missionary resources toward populations with genuine openness to the gospel. The client nation that aligns with this administration participates in blessing; the nation that fails to do so forfeits the historical opportunity.

9. Romans 10:14 opens four questions that require the client nation framework. The chain of calling — believing — hearing — heralding is not abstract logic. It describes the full operational sequence from individual faith back to the decision of a client nation to sponsor, fund, train, and deploy qualified gospel messengers. The detailed exegesis of these questions follows in the next session.

Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Five

Romans 10:14 — Client Nation Responsibility, the Doctrine of Heathenism, and the First Rhetorical Question

Romans 10:14 “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Consequently, how shall they call on Christ in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a proclaimer?

Romans 10 reaches its climactic second half with a series of four interlocking rhetorical questions addressing the responsibility of Israel as a client nation before God. These questions are not merely historical — they establish the principle that governs every client nation in every age, including the present one. The chapter begins its examination with verse 14, which introduces the first question: the problem of no gospel hearing among the nations.

I. Background: Israel as Client Nation and the Four Questions of Romans 10:14–15

The final half of Romans 10 addresses Jewish responsibility as a client nation to God. The Jews constituted four successive client nations in the Old Testament period: united Israel under the monarchy, the Northern Kingdom, the Southern Kingdom of Judah, and the restored postexilic community. Each bore the same dual mandate: dissemination of the gospel to surrounding Gentile nations, and custodianship of the developing Old Testament canon.

Paul structures his argument through four consecutive rhetorical questions, each of which answers the preceding one and presses the inquiry one step further back in the causal chain. The questions together delineate the complete sequence from the Gentile's inability to call upon the Lord all the way back to the failure of the client nation to send out qualified proclaimers. While the immediate historical reference is Israel, the logical structure applies to every national entity that God designates as a client nation. Two foundational concepts must be in place before the questions can be examined: the doctrine of the client nation, and the laws of divine establishment.

II. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:14a — The First Question

The Interrogative and Inferential Particles

The verse opens with the interrogative particle pōs (πῶς), used for a direct question to determine how something comes to be or how something should happen. With this particle Paul couples an inferential particle that signals the clause introduces a result from what precedes. The combined force is best rendered consequently, how — indicating that what follows is the logical result of the confession that all who call on the name of the Lord shall be saved (v. 13).

The Verb: epikaleō — to Call Upon

The main verb is the aorist middle subjunctive of epikaleō (ἐπικαλέω), meaning to call upon. This verb has already been established in the context (v. 13) as a synonym for saving faith — the act of calling upon the name of the Lord is coextensive with the act of believing. The aorist tense is constative, viewing the momentary act of faith in Christ as a single whole. The middle voice is the intensive middle, giving the verb an individualistic application: each person must personally exercise this act. The subjunctive mood is potential, implying future reference qualified by contingency.

The full clause reads: consequently, how shall they call on — with they (implicit subject in the Greek) referring to the Gentile peoples described throughout the preceding context as those who stand in need of salvation.

The Prepositional Phrase: eis hon — in whom

The object of calling is expressed by the preposition eis (εἰς) plus the accusative of the relative pronoun hos (ὅς), correctly translated in whom. In later Koine Greek, eis plus the accusative frequently absorbed the function of en plus the dative, and the usage here retains that idiomatic sense. The one called upon is Christ, implied from verse 13.

The Verb: pisteuō — to believe

The subordinate clause uses the constative aorist indicative of pisteuō (πιστεύω) plus the negative ouk (οὐκ): in whom they have not believed. The constative aorist views the entirety of saving faith but regards it from the standpoint of existing results; the English perfect tense best captures this: in whom they have not believed. The active voice with the negative indicates that the Gentiles are not producing the action of the verb. The cause of this failure is traced to malfunction within the client nation — the failure of believers to advance to maturity and to be sent out as qualified proclaimers. The indicative mood is the interrogative indicative, assuming that an actual answer to the question exists and is forthcoming. The full first question: Consequently, how shall they call on Christ in whom they have not believed?

III. The Two Problems Introduced by the First Question

The first question introduces two distinct problems, one more obvious than the other.

The Obvious Problem: No Belief Without Prior Calling

The more visible problem is this: no one, Jew or Gentile, can call upon the Lord — that is, confess saving faith in Christ — unless he has first believed in his right lobe. Calling upon the name of the Lord is the outward expression and synonym of an internal act of non-meritorious faith. The call is the result of belief; it cannot precede it. The question therefore presses back one logical step: how does belief come about? That question will be addressed by the second rhetorical question.

The Less Obvious Problem: Heathenism and the Absence of Gospel Hearing

The less obvious problem embedded in the first question is the problem of heathenism: the condition of large populations among whom there is no positive volition at the point of God consciousness. Where there is no positive volition, there is no mechanism by which God would send gospel information. Where there is no gospel information, there is no opportunity for saving faith. The question therefore raises the entire issue of what determines whether a Gentile nation receives a gospel witness at all — which is precisely the function of the client nation.

IV. The Doctrine of Heathenism

Definition and Etymology

The term heathen is not derived from Greek or Hebrew but from the Teutonic — specifically from the Gothic word hythe, meaning open country, the area outside of civilization. As a theological category, heathenism designates a nation, race, or people who do not acknowledge the God of the Bible. Their deities are consistently the product of imagination applied to observed phenomena: power seen in the elephant, lethal speed in the cobra, the forces of weather, the reproductive drives of the phallic cults. Invariably, heathen worship is directed toward objects inferior to mankind itself.

The Hebrew term is goi (גּוֹי), referring to the Gentile nations other than Israel. The Greek equivalent is ta ethnē (τὰ ἔθνη), the nations. Heathenism in its theological sense is not a primitive stage of religion that precedes revelation; it is the reversion that follows the rejection of revelation. Revelation existed first. Heathenism is its aftermath.

Heathenism as Salvation Maladjustment

Romans 1:18 establishes the doctrinal baseline: For the wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and anti-justice suppression of the truth. Heathenism is the condition of those who suppress the gospel through refusal to make the salvation adjustment to the justice of God. This maladjustment occurs at one of two critical points: at God consciousness or at gospel hearing. The doctrine of heathenism directly addresses the question posed by those unfamiliar with these principles: what about those who have never heard? Do they have no chance?

God Consciousness

God consciousness is that point at which a human being becomes aware of the existence of God through the function of his own mentality. This awareness is reached by rational introspection, anthropological inference from moral conscience, ontological inference from the concept of absolute perfection, teleological inference from design in the universe, and cosmological inference from cause and effect. The design of the universe — from the structure of the atom to the arrangement of galaxies — demands a designer. The moral structure of society demands an absolute source of righteousness beyond the relative moral impulses of the human soul.

God consciousness constitutes accountability. It varies with culture, language, environment, and mental capacity. Those who are mentally incapable of reaching accountability — infants who die, those born with severe cognitive limitations — are saved through the justice of God on the basis of condemnation at birth being resolved by the work of Christ. This is consistent with the teaching of 2 Samuel 12:23 and the imputation doctrine developed earlier in Romans.

The operative principle: if any member of the human race, regardless of geographical isolation or linguistic barrier, reaches God consciousness and has positive volition — a genuine desire for relationship with God — then God will provide the necessary gospel information through which that person can make the salvation adjustment to the justice of God. This is taught in Jeremiah 29:13 — 'You will seek me and find me when you search for me with all your heart.' John 7:17 — 'If anyone is willing to do his will, he shall know the doctrine.' Acts 17:27 — 'That they should seek God, if perhaps they might grope for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us.'

The Historical Record: No People Left Without Witness

The claim that entire peoples have been abandoned without any gospel opportunity is refuted by the historical record. The epistle of Pliny the Younger to the Emperor Trajan documents Christians throughout the provinces of Asia Minor in the early second century. The gospel reached Africa via Tyrian captives who led the Queen of Abyssinia to faith. Thaddaeus conducted missionary work in Persia, where he discovered that Matthew had already been there before him — his gospel was already in circulation. Around A.D. 190, Pantaenus of Alexandria traveled to India and found believers who possessed the Gospel of Matthew. The Nestorians evangelized China in the sixth century, a fact confirmed by the discovery of the Sian-Fu tablets in Chensi province.

The history of missionary expansion further demonstrates the client nation principle in operation across successive national entities. Ireland served as a missionary base through Columba (521–596), who evangelized Scotland and established the missionary school on the island of Iona. Columbanus (543–615) crossed into Germany and Switzerland. Willibrord (657–739) evangelized Holland and Denmark. Boniface (680–755) worked in Hesse and Saxony and is recorded as having brought over 100,000 persons to faith in twenty years of ministry in Germany; he was martyred at age seventy-five on the shores of the Zuider Zee, his head resting on a Bible. Ansgar was sent to Denmark by Louis the Pious of France, converted King Harold of Denmark, and pressed on to Sweden where he eventually led King Olaf to faith. Norway received the gospel from England in the tenth century. Ulfilas (311–388) translated the entire Bible into Gothic, omitting only Samuel and Kings out of concern that their warfare narratives would inflame an already warlike people. Cyril and Methodius (815–855) evangelized among the Slavic peoples.

At each stage, a stabilized national base served as the sending entity. The doctrine of divine justice underlies the entire pattern: God cannot compromise his justice; therefore no human being to whom he has imputed human life has ever been overlooked. Unlimited atonement means that all sins of every human being were imputed to Christ and judged on the cross. Divine sovereignty means he is not willing that any should perish but that all should come to a change of attitude. The doctrine of God consciousness provides the mechanism by which positive volition anywhere in the world triggers divine provision of gospel information.

Heathenism and the Vacuum of the Soul

When a person — or a culture — says no to truth at the point of God consciousness, the result is heathenism in the mind, which overflows into heathenism in behavior. The soul cannot survive without the entrance of truth. When truth is rejected, a vacuum is created that draws in darkness. The soul that has no doctrinal content has no standard capable of resisting the inflow of destructive influences. Heathenism then requires a substitute for truth, which it finds in the glorification of the trivial and the irrational. The pattern described in Romans 1:21–32 is not merely historical; it describes the progressive stages of any society that sustains negative volition toward the truth of God.

V. The Client Nation and the Missionary Mandate

The first question of Romans 10:14 — how shall they call on Christ in whom they have not believed? — introduces a logical chain that traces the problem of unevangelized peoples back to a single source: the spiritual condition of the client nation. Positive volition at God consciousness anywhere in the world creates a divine obligation, discharged through the normal historical mechanism of missionary activity sent from a stable client nation base.

The quality of the missionary is therefore not incidental but determinative. A missionary represents not only the gospel but the entire apparatus of the client nation's spiritual output. The missionary must have spiritual maturity, not merely theological education. Maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul produces the spiritual flexibility, genuine humility, and cross-cultural wisdom required. Spiritual maturity is not acquired quickly; it results from sustained daily intake of doctrine over years, cracking the maturity barrier and advancing through supergrace toward the ultra-supergrace level at which maximum production occurs.

The prerequisite is equally applicable at home: a person who lacks the courage and doctrinal confidence to present the gospel in his own language and cultural context will not gain those capacities by crossing an ocean. The linguistic, cultural, and social barriers of foreign missionary work are multiplied versions of the barrier that exists in ordinary evangelism. Spiritual cowardice, cultural inflexibility, and an attitude of national or cultural superiority are each disqualifying. True humility — not the performance of deference but the genuine orientation of the soul that comes through perception of doctrine and undeserved suffering — is indispensable.

The supporting structure of the client nation includes those believers who do not go to the field but who advance spiritually and provide financial undergirding for those who do. The pivot of mature believers within the nation is what sustains the nation's existence under logistical grace and makes continued missionary activity possible. The existence of a congregation of believers positive toward doctrine is not incidental to the survival of a client nation — it is the mechanism by which logistical grace is extended to that nation.

VI. Preview: The Second Question

The second question — how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? — will be examined in the following chapter. It presses the inquiry one step further back: the problem is not merely absence of calling, but absence of the prior condition that makes calling possible. Belief requires hearing. Hearing requires a proclaimer. A proclaimer requires sending. And sending requires a functional client nation. The rhetorical structure of Paul's argument moves from effect back through causes in sequence, each question answering the one before it, until the full responsibility of the client nation is established.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Five

1. The four questions of Romans 10:14–15 form a single logical unit. Each question is both an answer to the previous and a premise for the next, tracing the chain of causation from the Gentile's inability to call on Christ all the way back to the failure of the client nation to send qualified proclaimers.

2. The verb epikaleō is a synonym for saving faith. Calling upon the name of the Lord is not a separate act from believing; it is the expression and synonym of the non-meritorious act of faith in Christ. The constative aorist views the act as a single whole; the intensive middle emphasizes its personal, individualistic application.

3. The first question introduces two problems simultaneously. The more obvious problem is that no one can call upon Christ without first having believed. The less obvious but equally critical problem is the condition of heathenism — the absence of positive volition at the point of God consciousness — which determines whether any gospel witness reaches a given population.

4. Heathenism is not the original condition of mankind but a reversion from revelation. Revelation existed first. Heathenism results from sustained rejection of the truth available at God consciousness. The vacuum created by rejection of truth is filled by the darkness of heathen thought and behavior.

5. No human being has ever been without a chance of salvation. The justice of God, unlimited atonement, divine sovereignty, and the doctrine of God consciousness together guarantee that every person who reaches accountability and has positive volition will receive the gospel information necessary to make the salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

6. God consciousness constitutes accountability. It varies with culture, language, environment, and cognitive capacity. Those who die before reaching accountability — infants, those incapable of rational volition — are saved through the justice of God on the basis of the work of Christ.

7. The historical record confirms that no people has been left without a witness. From Persia to India, from China to Scandinavia, from Africa to the Gothic peoples north of the Danube, missionary activity sent from successive client nations has reached every major people group. Where positive volition existed, God provided the means.

8. The client nation principle rotates across different national entities across history. Ireland, Scotland, England, France, Germany, and others served as the missionary base in successive eras. The quality of the missionaries produced by each client nation correlated directly with the spiritual condition of the pivot within that nation.

9. Missionary quality is a function of spiritual maturity, not educational credential alone. Maximum doctrine resident in the soul produces the spiritual flexibility, genuine humility, cross-cultural wisdom, and courage that effective missionary service requires. No believer is qualified for the mission field before achieving a substantial level of spiritual growth through sustained doctrine intake.

10. The pivot of mature believers is the mechanism of national preservation under logistical grace. The continued existence of a client nation is not determined by its political leadership or military capacity but by the presence of a body of believers who are positive toward doctrine and advancing toward spiritual maturity. This is the theological basis for the survival of any nation that God designates as a client nation.

Where positive volition exists at God consciousness, God provides the necessary gospel information for the salvation adjustment to the justice of God.
heathenism Theologically: the condition of a nation or people that does not acknowledge the God of the Bible, resulting from rejection of revelation at the point of God consciousness. Etymology: Gothic hythe, open country. The reversion of the unbeliever; salvation maladjustment to the justice of God. Described in Romans 1:18–32 and 2 Peter 2.
salvation adjustment Instantaneous, non-repeatable act of faith in Christ by which the sinner is permanently reconciled to the justice of God. The justice of God is satisfied by the imputation and judgment of the believer's sins to Christ on the cross; the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer at the moment of faith. Contrasted with salvation maladjustment (heathenism), which suppresses the truth through refusal to believe.
client nation A national entity designated by God to serve as the custodian and disseminator of divine revelation, including the canon of Scripture and the gospel. Israel functioned as four successive client nations in the Old Testament period. The health and missionary output of a client nation depend upon the presence of a pivot of mature believers and the spiritual growth of immature believers advancing toward maturity.
pivot The body of mature believers within a client nation whose adjustment to the justice of God through spiritual growth sustains the divine blessing extended to that nation under logistical grace. The size and spiritual depth of the pivot determines the degree to which a nation is preserved and used by God in history.
logistical grace God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued function in the plan of God. Extended to the client nation as a whole on the basis of the presence of the pivot, sustaining the nation's survival even when its political and social trajectory is otherwise adverse.

Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Six

Romans 10:14b — The Second Rhetorical Question: Faith, Hearing, and the Missionary Mandate of the Client Nation

Romans 10:14b “And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (ESV)
Corrected translation: Furthermore, how shall they believe in Christ about whom they have not heard?

This chapter continues the verse-by-verse exposition of Romans 10:14, picking up at the second of three successive rhetorical questions Paul deploys as a debater's technique. The first question established that no one can call upon Christ without prior faith. The second question — examined here — drives the logical progression one step further: faith itself is impossible without prior hearing, and hearing is impossible without a communicator sent from a client nation. The exegesis moves from grammar to missionary theology, addressing the nature of the client nation, the primacy of evangelism, and the conditions for divine guidance on the mission field.

I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:14b

The second question opens with the same interrogative particle πώς (pōs), 'how,' which governed the first question, maintaining the formal structure of the deliberative series. Joined to it is the post-positive conjunctive particle δέ (de), used here not adversatively but transitionally, best rendered 'furthermore' rather than 'but' or 'now.' The particle signals a rational and logical advance within the sequence, not a contrast.

The verb is the aorist active subjunctive of pisteuō (πιστεύω), 'to believe.' The constative aorist gathers the entire act of believing in Christ into one entirety, viewing it as a single event rather than a process. The active voice indicates that the Gentiles produce the action — the volitional act of faith — on the principle of efficacious grace. The subjunctive mood is deliberative, a standard feature of the rhetorical question series Paul is constructing: the deliberative subjunctive in a sequence of rhetorical questions sets up a logical progression used to prove a point by successive demonstration.

The relative clause 'about whom they have not heard' uses the objective genitive singular of the relative pronoun hos (οὗ), correctly translated 'about whom.' The verb of the subordinate clause is the aorist active indicative of akouō (ἀκούω), 'to hear,' negated by ouk (οὐκ), the standard negative for the indicative mood. The culminative aorist views the entire period of common grace — the hearing of the gospel through missionary activity — in its entirety, but regards it from the standpoint of its existing result: the Gentiles have not heard, and the existing condition is therefore one of ignorance of Christ.

Corrected translation of the second question in full: 'Furthermore, how shall they — that is, the Gentiles — believe in Christ about whom they have not heard?' The question is not a request for information. It is a debater's move, establishing irrefutably that faith presupposes hearing, and hearing presupposes a communicator.

II. The Logical Sequence: Common Grace Precedes Efficacious Grace

Paul's second question establishes a strict theological sequence within the ordo salutis as it applies to the evangelization of the Gentile world. The sequence has three irreversible steps.

First, God consciousness arises in every human being as the result of general revelation — the evidence of creation and the inner moral sense — sufficient to produce positive or negative volition toward the existence of God. This was treated at length in Romans 1:18–21. Second, the gospel must be communicated to those who have responded positively at God consciousness. This communication is common grace: the provision of the message of Christ to human ears. Third, the individual exercises faith in Christ — efficacious grace — and is saved. This third step, calling on the name of the Lord (Romans 10:13), was the subject of the first rhetorical question.

The second rhetorical question locks in the indispensable role of step two. Common grace — hearing the gospel — precedes believing in Christ. Efficacious grace cannot operate in a vacuum of information. The Gentile living in heathenism has no access to the message of Christ from within heathenism itself. No system of indigenous religious thought within a non-client nation can generate the gospel. The communicator must come from outside.

III. The Client Nation as the Source of Missionary Communication

The second question therefore implies a fourth element in the sequence: the client nation. A client nation is a national entity in a given historical epoch that has been designated by God as the base from which His word is communicated to the surrounding world. Without a functioning client nation, there is no missionary base, no evangelism, and no salvation adjustment available to those at positive volition in heathen lands.

In the Old Testament dispensation, the client nation was Israel — first united under David and Solomon, then divided into the Northern and Southern Kingdoms, and finally reduced to the Southern Kingdom of Judah alone. Gentiles who heard the gospel in that era did so because mature Jewish believers went out from Israel as communicators, presenting the God of Israel and His coming Messiah as the only Savior. Paul himself, as the apostle to the Gentiles, was the last great missionary of client nation Israel. His execution marked the end of that era: within two years of his death, the fifth cycle of divine discipline fell on Israel in A.D. 70, and the nation was removed from history as a client nation. The Roman Empire — not the Republic, which had long since transitioned to imperial rule — succeeded Israel as the client nation of the Church Age for the following centuries.

The United States functions in this role in the current epoch of history. The responsibilities that fall to a client nation are therefore directly applicable to American believers in this generation.

IV. The Nature and Priority of the Missionary Calling

A. Evangelism as the Primary Mandate

The exegetical logic of Paul's second question establishes the absolute priority of evangelism in missionary activity. The purpose for which God leads a missionary to a foreign field is the communication of the gospel to those at positive volition at God consciousness. Every other activity — practical assistance in agriculture, engineering, medicine, or infrastructure — is subordinate to and derivative from that primary purpose. Such ancillary contributions are not inherently wrong; they reflect the believer's broader responsibilities. But they do not constitute the missionary's defining mandate. The problem faced by the heathen is spiritual. The solution must be spiritual. The gospel is spiritual phenomenon.

B. Evangelism and Doctrine: The Necessary Sequence

A persistent tension in missionary strategy pits mass evangelism against what has been called the indigenous approach — the training of native converts to evangelize their own people. Both represent legitimate and necessary functions, but their proper relationship is sequential, not alternative.

Evangelism must come first. An indigenous missionary movement cannot be initiated without believers, and believers are produced only through evangelism. Organizations or methodologies that emphasize indigenous development at the expense of initial evangelism invert the necessary order. Equally, however, evangelism that produces converts without providing for their doctrinal development condemns those converts to spiritual immaturity. A missionary who spends a decade in a given location and produces a thousand converts, then moves on without establishing any structure for their continued growth, has accomplished a fraction of what could be accomplished if those converts were trained, organized into a local church, and sent out as communicators themselves.

The historical record of the China Inland Mission illustrates this dynamic. Missionaries of exceptional dedication produced substantial numbers of converts across widely dispersed locations. Where converts were then gathered, taught, and organized into functioning local churches capable of reproducing themselves, the long-term multiplication was exponential. Where converts were left without doctrinal structure, they remained spiritual infants, unable to fulfill the communication role the second rhetorical question demands. The failure was not of evangelism itself but of the absence of the next step.

The transition from itinerant evangelism to the establishment of a local church requires a corresponding transition in spiritual gifts. The gift of evangelism, which enables sustained and fruitful proclamation to unbelievers, is distinct from the gift of pastor-teacher, which equips a communicator to feed and develop an established body of believers. An evangelist who continues in a pastoral role after a local church is established wastes the gift and limits its impact. The evangelist should move to the next field of positive volition; a pastor-teacher should take over the local congregation. This division of function according to spiritual gift is the practical resolution of the evangelism-versus-indigenous debate.

C. Divine Guidance and the Missionary's Location

Only God in His omniscience knows at any given moment in history where positive volition at God consciousness exists in the Gentile world. This is not information accessible to any human being through research, demographic analysis, or emotional impression. It is available only through divine guidance to a qualified, spiritually mature believer. The consequence is that the single most important operational requirement for a missionary — beyond language ability, cultural adaptability, doctrinal preparation, and personal character — is sensitivity to the leading of God the Holy Spirit regarding location.

A missionary may be genuinely called to missionary work and may possess all the requisite preparation, yet find himself in the wrong country at the wrong time. The absence of visible fruit over a sustained period does not automatically indicate that the missionary is in the wrong place; God frequently tests through apparent unproductivity before opening a door of extraordinary opportunity. Patrick of Scotland, sent to Ireland as a missionary, is a historical example: a man who persisted through opposition and ultimately led an extraordinary number of people to faith in Christ within a single generation — without any connection to the Roman ecclesiastical structure that later claimed his legacy.

The missionary must therefore hold his location with flexibility. Historical events have repeatedly closed entire fields — the communist consolidation of China after World War II, for instance, expelled the entire missionary community and forced a wholesale reassessment of field assignments. Missionaries who had invested years in language study and relationships with a particular people were compelled to determine whether God had reassigned them to an entirely different field. The capacity to make that transition without spiritual collapse or bitterness depends directly on the level of doctrinal maturity the missionary carries into the situation. A missionary operating primarily from emotional investment rather than Bible doctrine will find such disruptions catastrophic. A missionary grounded in doctrine can recognize the closing of one door as the opening of another and relocate without loss of momentum.

V. The Client Nation's Future Missionary Responsibility

The exegetical context of Romans 10:14 carries immediate application to the current historical moment. Dialectical materialism — the ideological foundation of communist regimes — systematically suppresses any acknowledgment of God's existence and trains populations from childhood to deny divine reality. Yet neither state ideology nor sustained cultural pressure can permanently extinguish the capacity for God consciousness. The evidence of creation continues to function. The inner moral sense continues to operate. The ideological vacuum created by the failure of materialist systems to satisfy the deepest human questions produces, across generations, an intensified positive volition that no state apparatus can wholly contain.

The consequence, from the standpoint of Romans 10:14, is that the fields presently under communist control represent the greatest concentration of positive volition at God consciousness that exists in the world. When political conditions shift — as they inevitably do under the pressure of historical forces — the spiritual opportunity that opens will exceed anything in the history of missions. The client nation that is prepared, with mature believers trained in doctrine and genuinely led by the Spirit, will be in a position to respond to that opportunity with maximum effect.

Preparation requires decades of sustained doctrinal teaching, the production of spiritually mature believers from whose ranks God calls missionaries, and the financial capacity of an advancing Christian community to support sustained missionary work. The second rhetorical question of Romans 10:14 therefore speaks not only to Paul's first-century audience but to any generation of believers living within a functioning client nation: the hearing of the gospel by those at positive volition depends upon whether prepared communicators are sent.

Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Six

1. The deliberative subjunctive in a rhetorical question series: Paul's series of rhetorical questions in Romans 10:14 employs the deliberative subjunctive not to elicit information but to construct a logical sequence. Each question picks up a key term from its predecessor — 'call upon' leads to 'believe,' 'believe' leads to 'hear' — building an irrefutable chain of reasoning toward a predetermined conclusion.

2. Common grace precedes efficacious grace: Hearing the gospel is common grace — the provision of the message of Christ to those capable of receiving it. Efficacious grace — the saving act of faith in response to that message — cannot operate without the prior provision of common grace. The sequence is irreversible: God consciousness, then hearing, then faith.

3. The Gentiles in heathenism cannot supply the gospel from within heathenism: No system of indigenous Gentile religious thought generates the gospel. The communicator must come from outside — from a client nation — because the message of Christ has no native source in heathenism.

4. The client nation is fundamentally a missionary nation: The most strategically significant function of a client nation in any historical epoch is its role as the base from which missionaries are sent to fields of positive volition. Prosperity, freedom, and political stability serve this missionary purpose; they are not ends in themselves.

5. Evangelism is always the primary missionary mandate: The problem of the heathen is spiritual; the solution must be spiritual. Ancillary humanitarian contributions by missionaries are not prohibited, but they are always secondary to the proclamation of the gospel. A missionary who neglects evangelism in favor of social improvement has inverted Paul's sequence.

6. Evangelism and the indigenous movement are sequential, not alternative: The indigenous approach — training native believers to evangelize their own people — presupposes a prior body of converts. Evangelism must come first. Once converts exist and a local church is established, the transition to indigenous multiplication is not only permissible but necessary for maximum doctrinal and numerical growth.

7. The transition from evangelism to pastoring requires a transition in gift: The gift of evangelism and the gift of pastor-teacher are distinct. An evangelist who remains in a pastoral role after a local church is established limits both his own gift and the growth of the congregation. Proper stewardship of spiritual gifts requires recognizing when one phase of ministry has concluded and another must begin.

8. Omniscience alone knows where positive volition exists: The location of positive volition at God consciousness in any generation is known only to God. Missionary placement therefore demands a higher degree of sensitivity to divine guidance than any other form of Christian service. Doctrinal maturity is the precondition for that sensitivity; emotional impression is an inadequate and unreliable substitute.

9. Missionary flexibility is a doctrinal virtue: When historical events close a mission field — through political upheaval, expulsion, or conquest — the mature missionary is able to relocate without spiritual collapse. The capacity for this flexibility is a direct function of the missionary's doctrinal foundation. Operating from emotion rather than doctrine produces rigidity disguised as faithfulness.

10. Paul as the last great missionary of client nation Israel: Paul's role as apostle to the Gentiles represented the terminal expression of Israel's missionary mandate. Within two years of his execution, the fifth cycle of divine discipline fell on the nation, and Israel was removed from history as a client nation. The Roman Empire succeeded Israel in that role for the subsequent centuries of the Church Age.

11. Communist ideology creates intensified positive volition: The systematic suppression of God consciousness under materialist ideology does not eliminate the innate human capacity for God consciousness; it intensifies it across generations. Fields currently closed to missionary activity by communist regimes represent a concentrated reservoir of positive volition that will require the most prepared missionaries in history when those fields open.

12. Preparation, not zeal, is the precondition for effective missionary work: Zeal without doctrine produces burned-out missionaries who accomplish a fraction of what prepared, mature communicators achieve. The doctrinal and personal preparation required for effective missionary work is at least as demanding as that required for pastoral ministry — and in some respects more so, given the additional requirements of cultural flexibility, language acquisition, and sensitivity to divine guidance in an unfamiliar environment.

Glossary

Glossary

Term Greek / Transliteration Definition
pōs πώς pōs — how Interrogative adverb used to introduce direct and rhetorical questions. In Romans 10:14, Paul uses it three successive times as the structural marker of his deliberative rhetorical series.
de δέ de — furthermore, now Post-positive conjunctive particle. In Romans 10:14b, used transitionally rather than adversatively, signaling a rational advance within the logical sequence of rhetorical questions rather than a contrast.
pisteuō πιστεύω pisteuō — to believe, to have faith in The standard New Testament verb for saving faith. In Romans 10:14b, the constative aorist active subjunctive gathers the entire act of believing in Christ into a single event, emphasizing the volitional nature of faith as non-meritorious trust in Christ alone.
akouō ἀκούω akouō — to hear To hear, to perceive by the ear. In Romans 10:14b, the culminative aorist active indicative with the negative ouk: 'they have not heard.' The culminative aspect views the entire period of missionary communication in its entirety and regards it from the standpoint of its existing result — the absence of the gospel message.
deliberative subjunctive deliberative subjunctive A grammatical construction in which the subjunctive mood appears in a question to express a logical or moral deliberation. In Romans 10:14, Paul's three successive deliberative subjunctives form a rhetorical chain in which each question establishes the precondition for the next, driving the argument toward the necessity of the missionary.
common grace common grace God's provision of the gospel message to those capable of receiving it — hearing as the precondition for faith. Distinguished from efficacious grace (the saving act of faith itself). In the ordo salutis of Romans 10:13–15, common grace (hearing) precedes efficacious grace (believing).
efficacious grace efficacious grace The divine provision by which faith in Christ results in salvation. Non-meritorious on the part of the believer: faith is the non-meritorious instrument, not the basis, of justification. Efficacious grace cannot operate without prior common grace — the hearing of the gospel.
client nation client nation A national entity designated by God in a given historical epoch as the base from which His word is communicated to the surrounding Gentile world. In the Old Testament, client nation Israel; in the early Church Age, the Roman Empire; in the current epoch, the United States. The client nation provides the political freedom, economic base, and missionary personnel necessary for world evangelization.
God consciousness God consciousness The innate human awareness of the existence of a divine being, produced by general revelation — the evidence of creation and the inner moral sense. God consciousness is the first volitional decision point: positive response leads to gospel hearing; negative response constitutes suppression of truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18).
fifth cycle of discipline fifth cycle of discipline The terminal stage of national divine discipline, resulting in the complete historical destruction of a client nation through military conquest, dispersion, and the removal of divine protection. Applied to Israel in A.D. 70 through the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, ending Israel's role as a client nation for the duration of the Church Age.
indigenous missions indigenous missions The missionary strategy of training native converts to evangelize their own people, establish local churches, and send out native pastors. Distinguished from itinerant evangelism. Theologically and strategically necessary, but presupposes a prior body of converts produced by initial evangelism from an outside source.

Chapter Six Hundred Seventy-Seven

Romans 10:14 — Common Grace, Efficacious Grace, and Missionary Function of the Client Nation

Romans 10:8–14 “But what does it say? 'The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart' (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim); because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. For the Scripture says, 'Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.' For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him. For 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (ESV)
Corrected translation: But what does faith righteousness say? Quoting from Deuteronomy 30:14: 'The message is near you — in your mouth and in your right lobe.' That is the message of faith which we proclaim. Namely, if you will confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, and if you will believe with your right lobe that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For by means of the right lobe mankind believes, resulting in the imputed righteousness of God; and by means of the mouth mankind makes a statement to God regarding salvation. For the Scripture says, quoting Isaiah 28:16: 'Whoever believes in Him will not be disappointed.' For there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for the same Lord of all is rich in logistical grace to all who call on Him. Quoting Joel 2:32: 'Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.' Consequently, how shall they — the Gentiles — call on Christ in whom they have not believed? Furthermore, how shall they believe in Christ about whom they have not heard? Furthermore, how shall they hear without a missionary?

Romans 10 continues Paul's exposition of the contrast between faith righteousness and works righteousness. Having established in verses 8–13 that salvation is as near as the right lobe of the soul and the mouth — and that this applies without distinction to Jew and Gentile alike — Paul arrives in verse 14 at a threefold rhetorical impasse. The three questions of verse 14 constitute one of the most architecturally precise arguments in the New Testament: a descending chain of logical necessity that moves from efficacious grace, to common grace, to the missionary function of the client nation. This chapter works through those three questions and the doctrinal framework they establish.

I. The Rhetorical Architecture of Romans 10:14

Verse 14 opens with the inferential conjunction translated 'consequently' or 'how then,' signaling that what follows is a logical deduction from the universal accessibility of salvation proclaimed in verses 9–13. Paul deploys three successive questions, each introduced by the interrogative particle

by the interrogative particle pōs (πῶς), used here not in its simple interrogative sense but as a rhetorical device of logical progression. Each pōs tightens the chain: the first question presupposes the second, and the second presupposes the third. The effect is a structured reductio that exposes layer after layer of deficiency in the mission field — not to condemn the Gentiles who have not heard, but to indict the failure of the client nation that should have sent the message.

This debating technique — posing sequential questions that compel assent at each step before delivering the conclusive blow — was a recognized device of sophisticated rhetorical argument in the ancient world. Paul employs it here with exceptional economy: three questions in a single verse establish the entire logical structure that the remainder of the passage unpacks.

The Three Questions

Question One: 'Consequently, how shall they — the Gentiles — call on Christ in whom they have not believed?' This is the question of efficacious grace. Calling on the Lord (verse 13, quoting Joel 2:32) presupposes prior faith. You cannot acknowledge to God that Jesus is Lord and Savior if you have not first believed in the right lobe of the soul. The mouth gives voice to what the right lobe has already received. Where there is no faith, there is no genuine calling.

Question Two: 'Furthermore, how shall they believe in Christ about whom they have not heard?' This is the question of common grace. Faith in the right lobe requires content: the gospel must be presented and received before the soul can exhale faith in Christ. No one believes in a person about whom they know nothing. The unbeliever may reach God-consciousness — a general awareness that God exists — but God-consciousness is not salvation. At best, unaided God-consciousness produces deism: a belief in deity without knowledge of the person and work of Christ. Gospel hearing must precede gospel faith.

Question Three: 'Furthermore, how shall they hear without a missionary?' This is the question of client-nation function. The gospel does not reach foreign peoples by atmospheric diffusion. It requires a human messenger who crosses a national boundary — a believer who leaves the client nation and goes to a foreign country to present the message. The absence of such a messenger is a malfunction of the client nation, not a failure of divine provision.

II. The Vocabulary of Verse 14: Common Grace and Efficacious Grace

Common Grace

Common grace is the Holy Spirit acting as a human spirit to give the unbeliever genuine perception of the gospel. The unbeliever — the natural man, the psychikos anthrōpos (ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος) — does not possess a human spirit and therefore cannot, by his own faculties, receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). The gospel is spiritual phenomena; the unbeliever lacks the receptor. The Holy Spirit bridges this gap by supplying, temporarily and for the duration of gospel presentation, the functional equivalent of a human spirit. This is the inhale: the gospel enters the soul with genuine comprehension. This temporary ministry is common grace because it is extended to all who hear the gospel, without distinction.

Efficacious Grace

Efficacious grace is the exhale: faith in Jesus Christ arising from the right lobe of the soul. The Greek construction in verse 10 — kardia gar pisteuetai eis dikaiosynēn (καρδίᾳ γὰρ πιστεύεται εἰς δικαιοσύνην) — establishes that it is 'by means of the right lobe' (the heart, the kardia, καρδία) that mankind believes, resulting in the imputed righteousness of God. Faith is non-meritorious: it is the simple, volitional response of the right lobe to the content received through common grace. Because faith has no intrinsic merit, the righteousness that results is entirely from God — it is imputed, not earned. This is the salvation adjustment to the justice of God.

The Logical Sequence

Common grace must precede efficacious grace. No one believes in Christ until the gospel has been presented and comprehended. The sequence is fixed: missionary evangelism → gospel hearing → common grace (Holy Spirit gives perception) → faith in the right lobe → efficacious grace → salvation adjustment to the justice of God. No step in this sequence may be skipped, and no step may be reversed.

III. The Third Question: The Missionary and the Client Nation

Exegesis of the Third Question

The third question introduces two critical grammatical features. First, the adverb chōris (χωρίς), functioning here as an improper preposition — 'apart from' or 'without' — governs the genitive case of what follows. Second, the word commonly translated 'preacher' in the King James Version is not a noun but an articular present active participle from the verb kēryssō (κηρύσσω), meaning to herald, to proclaim, to announce publicly. The participle is used substantively — that is, as a noun — and should be rendered 'the one who proclaims' or, in context, 'a missionary.' The full clause: 'Furthermore, how shall they hear apart from one who proclaims — a missionary?'

This is not a passage about personal witnessing. It is not addressed to the evangelist speaking to his own congregation. By interpretation, the figure here is the missionary: a believer who departs from a client nation and crosses a national boundary to present the gospel in a foreign country. That is the referent of the participle, and every application of this verse that departs from that referent misses the passage's theological target.

What Constitutes a Missionary

A missionary, by definition, is a believer who leaves a client nation and goes to a foreign nation to accomplish two objectives in sequence: first, to evangelize — to present the gospel and call for faith in Christ; and second, to establish an indigenous local function, a self-sustaining body of believers operating under local leadership with locally appropriate forms. The missionary does not transplant the cultural norms of the sending nation. Flexibility under the honor code is essential: the missionary does not make cultural conformity a condition of the gospel. Social structures, customs, and practices that are not themselves violations of divine establishment are not the missionary's assignment to reform.

The missionary must be a believer of some spiritual maturity — or advancing toward it. Effective missionary function requires the honor code, doctrinal orientation, flexibility, language acquisition, and the capacity to discern what is culturally negotiable from what is doctrinally non-negotiable. These are not qualities produced by enthusiasm or zeal alone; they require the sustained intake of Bible doctrine over time.

The Client Nation's Responsibility

Only believers within a client nation support the missionary enterprise. This is a categorical distinction. Unbelievers within a client nation benefit from establishment principles — freedom, law, protection — and are themselves objects of evangelism within the nation's borders. But unbelievers do not and cannot sustain missionary activity to foreign nations. That is the exclusive function of the believing community within the client nation. A large and spiritually advancing corps of believers within the client nation is the prerequisite for a functioning missionary movement. When that corps is reduced by unbelief, reversionism, or negative volition toward doctrine, the missionary movement contracts proportionately.

The corollary follows: the spiritual condition of the pivot — the body of mature believers within a client nation — directly determines the scope and effectiveness of that nation's missionary outreach. This is not a secondary matter of church programming; it is the primary expression of a client nation's reason for existence before God.

IV. Tongues, Missions, and the Warning to Israel

The gift of tongues (glōssai, γλῶσσαι) was a temporary sign gift operative between Pentecost (AD 30) and the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70). The gift consisted of the supernatural ability to speak an unlearned foreign human language for the purpose of gospel proclamation. It was not an ecstatic utterance; it was a foreign language — the very instrument of missionary activity.

The sign-function of tongues was directed toward Israel. The covenant structure of the Old Testament assigned to Israel — as the client nation — the responsibility of sending missionaries to the Gentile world. The missionary was to go from Israel to the nations, learning the language of the foreign people and presenting the gospel in their tongue. When, instead, foreign-born Jews returning to Jerusalem at Pentecost heard the gospel proclaimed in the languages of the Gentile diaspora by Galilean believers, the sign was unmistakable: Israel was no longer functioning as the sending client nation. The flow had reversed. Gentile languages were now being used to evangelize Jews on Jewish soil. This reversal was the divinely ordained warning that the fifth cycle of discipline — national destruction — was imminent.
